INTRODIJCTION. 

AT  the  suggestion  of   many  Old  Tonbridgians,   I  propose  to 
introduce  the  Eegister  by  giving  a  sketch  of  the  History  of 
the  Schooh 

The  beginnings  of  its  history  are  enveloped  in  some  mystery 
and  doubt.  It  is  an  undeniable  fact  that  Sir  Andrew  Judde 
obtained  from  King  Edward  VI.,  a  few  months  before  the  King's 
death,  in  1553,  a  Charter,  sanctioning  the  foundation  of  a  Free 
Grammar  School  at  Tonbridge.  But  how  soon  the  Founder  put 
his  plans  into  execution  we  have  been  unable  to  ascertain. 
Documentary  evidence  of  the  School's  existence  dates  back  to  the 
first  year  of  Queen  Elizabeth's  reign,  and  on  the  strength  of  this 
fact,  Dr.  Thomas  Knox,  the  first  historian  of  the  School,  has 
based  the  assertion  that  Sir  Andrew  Judde  held  his  scheme  in 
abeyance  during  the  religious  troubles  of  Queen  Mary's  reign. 
This  statement,  however,  is  a  mere  theory,  which  is  shown  to  be  a 
mistake  by  the  fact  that  the  Founder's  death  took  place  some 
months  before  the  death  of  Queen  Mary,  and  yet,  that,  in  his  will, 
he  mentions  the  School  as  in  working  condition.  The  docu- 
mentary evidence  to  which  we  have  alluded  commences,  in  fact, 
when  the  Skinners'  Company,  in  accordance  with  the  provisions  of 
Sir  Andrew's  will,  became  the  Trustees  of  the  School.  The  name 
of  the  first  Head  Master,  John  Proctor,  is  well  known,  as  he  is 
mentioned  in  connection  with  the  School  by  many  contemporary 
writers.  He  was  a  man  of  some  mark,  and  his  story  suggests, 
if  it  does  not  supply  with  certainty,  the  missing  date.  John 
Proctor  wrote  a  history  of  Wyat's  Eebellion,  which  took  place  in 
1554,  and  it  is  remarkable  that  almost  the  only  trivial  incident 
mentioned  in  the  book  is  the  following.  Eelating  how  one, 
Antony  Knevet,  started  from  Tonbridge  to  join  the  rebels,  the 
author  says  that  "  after  he  was  leapt  to  his  horse,  he  toke  one  by 
the  hand,  and  said :  '  fare  ye  well !  and  if  you  happe  to  heare  that 
I  am  taken,  never  beleve  it,  for  undoubtedlye  I  wyll  eyther  die  in 
the  felde,  or  achive  my  purpose.'  But  within  twenty-four  hours 
he  brake  his  promise,  and  ranne  awaye  no  faster  than  his  legges 
could  carye  him."  In  reading  this  episode,  one  cannot  help 
thinking  that  the  writer  himself  was  the  one  whom  Knevet  "  toke 
by  the  hand";  and,  if  John  Proctor  was  then  at  Tonbridge,  it 
was  almost  certainly  in  the  capacity  of  Head  Master  of  the 
School;  for  his  own  native  county  was  not  Kent  but  Dorsetshire. 

Introduction.  v. 

But  perhaps  the  foundation-stone  of  the  original  building,  which 
is  now  inserted  in  the  wall  over  the  door  of  the  Head  Master's 
house,  supplies  the  most  valuable  piece  of  evidence  as  to  the  date 
at  which  the  existence  of  the  School  actually  commenced  ;  for,  on 
the  stone  may  still  be  read  the  following  inscription,  "  This  Shole, 
made  bi  Sir  Andro  Judde,  Knight,  and  gevin  to  the  Company  of 
Skinners,  Ano  1553."  We  may  mention  as  a  fact  also  bearing  on 
the  date  of  the  foundation  of  the  School,  that  the  Skinners' 
account  books  for  the  year  1559-60  give  details  of  extensive  repairs 
in  the  School  building,  which  could  scarcely  have  been  necessary 
if  the  School  had  only  been  erected  in  1558.  Lastly,  John  Proctor 
attained  to  a  high  reputation  as  Head  of  the  School,  and  yet  his 
successor  was  appointed  in  1559.  Can  it  be  believed  that  John 
Proctor  could  have  become  eminent  as  Head  Master  of  Tonbridge 
if  he  had  reigned  only  a  single  year  ?  On  the  whole,  we  are 
forced  to  the  conclusion  that  the  School  was  actually  erected  and 
at  work  very  soon  after  the  original  Charter  was  granted. 

Under  the  first  three  Head  Masters  there  were  two  Scholars 
who  became  notable  men.  The  first  of  these  was  Francis  Thynne, 
a  renowned  antiquary,  and  a  man  learned  in  the  study  of 
Heraldry  and  Genealogy.  He  filled  successively  the  offices  of 
Blanche  Lyon  Poursuivant  and  Lancaster  Herald.  The  other 
was  Sir  Eobert  Heath,  a  great  Lawyer,  who  became  Chief  Justice 
of  the  Common  Pleas.  John  Stockwood,  the  third  Head  Master 
(1574-86),  wrote  several  educational  works,  which  had  a  great 
reputation  in  their  day.  For  one  of  these  books,  epigrams  in 
praise  of  their  Master  were  written  by  ten  of  his  pupils  at 
Tonbridge  School,  one  of  whom  was  William  Hatch,  who  was 
also  his  successor  in  the  Head  Master's  office.  Of  Hatch's  time 
at  the  School  very  little  is  known,  as  also  of  that  of  his  three 
immediate  successors.  In  1640,  Thomas  Home,  D.D.,  became 
Head  Master,  having  previously  held  the  same  position  at 
Leicester  Grammar  School.  He  wrote  several  educational  books, 
and  among  his  pupils  one  of  the  most  noteworthy  was  Thomas 
Cheeseman,  a  blind  scholar,  who,  in  spite  of  his  disability, 
obtained  a  Smythe  Exhibition  and  took  his  degree  at  Oxford. 
He  was  afterwards  ordained,  and  was,  for  a  time,  deprived  of 
his  living  in  Berkshire  and  imprisoned  at  Beading  for  Noncon- 
formity. In  1649  Dr.  Home  was  succeeded  by  Dr.  Nicholas 
Grey,  who  had  been  previously,  in  succession,  Head  Master  of 
Charterhouse  School,  of  Merchant  Taylors'  School,  and  of  Eton 
College,  from  which  last  office  he  was  ejected  in  the  troublous 
times  of  the  Commonwealth.  Dr.  Grey  was  succeeded  at 
Tonbridge  by  Mr,  John  Goad,  but  the  latter  held  the  office  for 

vi.  Introduction. 

only  two  years,  being  then  transferred  to  Merchant  Taylors' 
School,  where  he  remained  for  twenty  years.  Under  Mr.  Goad's 
successor,  Dr.  Christopher  Wase,  Thomas  Herbert,  eighth  Earl 
of  Pembroke,  was  educated  at  the  School.  He  is  noted  chiefly 
for  having  been  First  Plenipotentiary  of  England  at  the 
negotiations  which  preceded  the  Treaty  of  Eyswick.  Dr.  Wase 
was  followed  by  Thomas  Eoots,  who  had  formerly  been  a  Scholar 
and  Smythe  Exhibitioner.  Mr.  Boots'  Head-Mastership  seems 
to  have  been  a  period  of  depression  for  the  School,  as  the  annual 
Examiner  reports  again  and  again  that  there  are  ' '  no  Scholars 
fit  for  the  Universities."  We  also  find  that  the  Governors  made 
many  vain  attempts  to  get  rid  of  Mr.  Eoots,  but  whether  they 
at  last  succeeded,  or  whether  he  died  in  harness,  is  not  known. 
His  successor,  Eichard  Spencer,  held  office  for  nearly  thirty  years, 
and  wiote  some  educational  works,  which  had  a  high  reputation 
in  their  day.  At  length  he  retired,  and  James  Cawthorn 
took  his  place.  He  was  noted  for  his  severity,  and  his  ghost 
w^as  supposed  to  haunt  the  dormitory  of  the  old  School-building. 
One  of  his  pupils  was  George  x\usten,  the  father  of  Jane  Austen, 
the  novelist.  Another  was  Lord  Whitworth,  afterwards  noted 
as  the  ablest  diplomatist  of  his  time.  The  most  marked  incident 
of  his  career  was  when,  as  Ambassador  at  Paris  during  the  Peace 
of  Amiens,  he  was  twice  publicly  insulted  by  the  Emperor 
Napoleon.  Lord  Eardley  and  Colonel  James,  ancestor  of  the 
present  Colonel  James,  of  Ightham  Lodge  (who  is  also  an  Old 
Tonbridgian),  were  at  the  School  with  Lord  Whitworth.  Another 
of  Mr.  Cawthorn's  pupils  was  William  Woodfall,  better  known 
as  Memory  Woodfall,  w^ho  first  attempted,  with  any  success,  to 
report  the  debates  in  the  House  of  Commons.  He  was  also  the 
printer  of  the  "Letters  of  Junius."  After  Mr.  Cawthorn,  came 
Mr.  Johnson  Towers,  of  whose  times  nothing  noteworthy  is 
recorded.  On  the  retirement,  in  1770,  of  Mr.  Towers,  he  was 
succeeded  by  the  Eev.  Vicesimus  Knox,  the  first  of  three  members 
of  one  family,  who  successively  governed  the  School.  The  first 
Vicesimus  Knox  had  one  pupil  who  became  a  distinguished  man. 
This  was  Anthony  Hart,  who  in  course  of  time  was  appointed 
Lord  Chancellor  of  Leland.  The  second  Vicesimus  Knox  was  an 
author  of  some  mark ;  the  titles  of  his  principal  works  are 
"Liberal  Education,"  "Winter  Evenings,"  "Personal  Nobility," 
and  "The  Spirit  of  Despotism."  Several  men  of  distinction 
were  educated  under  the  second  Vicesimus  at  Tonbridge  School. 
Among  these  may  be  mentioned  three  brothers  named  Clarke,  of 
whom  the  first  was  the  great  traveller  ;  the  second,  an  author 
of  some  merit,  and  also  Lord  Nelson's  Chaplain  at  the  battle  of 

Introduction.  vii. 

Trafalgar ;  and  the  third,  a  Naval  Captain,  who  served  under 
Earl  St.  Vincent  and  Lord  Nelson.  Pierre  Dumoustier,  one  of 
Napoleon's  Generals,  was  also  at  Tonbridge  under  the  younger 
Dr.  V.  Knox,  and  was  so  attached  to  his  old  School  and  Master 
that  he  paid  a  visit  to  them  during  the  brief  interval  of  peace 
between  England  and  France,  known  as  the  Peace  of  Amiens. 
Sir  Sidney  Smith,  the  Admiral,  often  called  "the  Hero  of  Acre," 
was  yet  another  pupil  of  this  Head  Master,  as  was  Julius  Hare, 
the  author  of  "Guesses  at  Truth"  and  other  works,  and  Sir  Archi- 
bald Campbell,  who  became  a  military  commander  of  some  note. 
On  the  retirement  of  the  second  Vicesimus,  he  was  succeeded  by 
Dr.  Thomas  Knox,  his  son,  and  the  grandson  of  the  first  Vicesimus. 
Some  years  after  Dr.  Thomas's  accession,  he  raised  a  question 
as  to  the  government  of  the  School,  maintaining  that  the 
Skinners'  Company  were  only  the  Trustees  of  the  lands  and 
houses  bequeathed  by  the  Founder,  whereas  the  Company  held 
that  these  lands  were  their  absolute  property,  provided  that  they 
kept  up  the  School.  The  question  was  finally  decided  in 
accordance  with  Dr.  Thomas  Knox's  view,  and  soon  afterwards 
a  New  Scheme  was  drawn  up,  under  which  sixteen  Exhibitions 
to  the  Universities,  each  of  £100  a  year  for  four  years,  were 
instituted.  Under  Dr.  Thomas  Knox  were  several  Scholars  who 
have  risen  to  distinction,  most  of  whom  are  still  living.  Among 
these  may  be  mentioned  the  Bishop  of  Derry,  Bishop  Courtenay 
(formerly  of  Jamaica),  Canon  Eowsell,  Admiral  Courtenay,  Viscount 
Strangford,  and  Generals  Hassard,  Gott,  and  Jordan.  At  Dr. 
Thomas  Knox's  death  in  1843  Dr.  Welldon  became  Head  Master, 
and  held  the  office  for  thirty-three  years — a  period  of  steadily- 
increasing  prosperity,  which  witnessed  the  erection  of  the  Chapel 
(in  1859),  the  Cricket  Pavihon  (in  1860),  and  the  new  School 
Buildings  (in  1863).  Among  Dr.  Welldon's  principal  pupils  were 
the  Dean  of  Derry,  General  Henry  Brackenbury,  C.B.,  Colonel 
Charles  Brackenbury,  General  Septimus  Hodgson,  Major-General 
Sir  Henry  Collett,  K.C.B.,  Sir  Maxwell  Melvill,  E.  Cooper 
WilHs,  Q.C.,  and  the  Bishop  of  Brisbane.  From  1876  to  1890 
the  Eev.  T.  B.  Eowe  was  Head  Master,  in  whose  time  a  New 
Scheme  came  into  force,  and  also  the  Gymnasium  and  Science 
Buildings  were  erected.  On  Mr.  Eowe's  resignation,  he  was 
succeeded  by  the  Eev.  Joseph  Wood,  D.D.,  previously  Head 
Master  of  Leamington  College,  under  whom  the  number  of 
Scholars  has  risen  to  the  unexampled  figure  of  350.  The  last 
event  to  be  recorded  in  the  history  of  the  School  is  a  large 
extension  of  the  main  block  of  buildings,  the  foundations  for 
which  were  laid  in  the  Autumn  of  1892.

Henry  Fisher,  (F.),  a  servant  of  Sir  Andrew  Judd,  after  his

with  respect  to  Tonbridge  School,  but  also  himself  gave

of  which  they  were  to  provide  an  Exhibition  for  a  Ton- 
bridge  Scholar  at  Brasenose  College,  Oxford. 

Sir  Thomas  White,  (W.),  the  founder  of  St.  John's  College,  Oxford, 
provided  that,  "in  respect  of  the  great  love  we  did  bear 
Andrew  Judd,  Knight,  builder  of  the  Grammar  School 
there,"  one  of  the  fellowships  in  his  College  (which  were 
probationary  for  the  first  three  years)  should  always  be 
held  by  a  Scholar  of   Tonbridge  School. 

Sir  Thomas  Smythe,  (S.),  (grandson  of  Sir  Andrew  Judd),  founded 
in  1619  six  Exhibitions,  to  be  held  for  seven  years  at 
either  of  the  Universities  by  Scholars  from  Tonbridge 
School.

WooDFALL,  William.  A  Scholar  about  this  time.  He 
became  celebrated  as  a  Eeporter  of  the  debates  in  the 
Houses  of  Parliament.  No  notes  were  allowed  to  be

Woodfall  succeeded  in  giving  almost  verbatim  reports. 
While  at  School  he  had  first  shown  this  great  power  of 
memory.  One  evening  the  Head  Master  gave  him  a  book 
of  Homer  to  learn  by  heart.  Next  morning  Woodfall 
repeated  the  "Imposition"  without  missing  a  word.  He 
was  also  a  printer,  Tiie  "  Letters  of  Junius"  were  first 
issued  from  his  press.

Heath . . 18 CORRESPONDENCE . . . . 20 RECENT LITERATURE Donald R. S . teggles 28 OBITUARY: GEOFFREY H. PLATT .. 31 1The Birth Pangs of the Oystermouth Railway 

BY G. F. GABB In his latest book, The Mumbles Past and Present, a pioneering work and full of fascinating information, Norman Lewis Thomas describes briefly .the evolution of the Oystermouth Railway scheme. He maintains that Sir John Morris wanted a tramway to develop his Clyne collieries, but was opposed by a group led by Edward Martin who preferred a canal. The battle was waged in the columns of the Cambrian, and finally won by Morris in the House of Commons.' The fol-lowing account is an attempt to show that such an interpretation is (naturally) over-simplified, and to demonstrate that the issue was fought by different group-ings for different reasons. In the early years of the 19th Century the burgesses of Swansea were content for the town to develop as a port, but wanted to exclude industry in a bid to make the borough a fashionable resort. As a result, works and collieries blossomed just outside their jurisdiction under the shadow of Kilvay Hill, and along the banks of the Tawe in Landore, Morriston and Llansamlet. The tidal river had its limitations as a means of communication with the shipping places in the town; so Townsend's Waggonway was constructed about 1750, and John Smith's Canal in 1785, both serving the east side. On the west bank came the Swansea Canal in 1796, joining the river near the brewery. In addition, the Cwm Tramway served the Cwm and Pentre Collieries, terminating near the Pottery, perhaps a quarter of a mile upstream from the brewery, and close to the site of High Street Station. This tramway dated at least from 1771,2 and when the Swansea Canal was built, a tunnel was constructed to accommodate it near the canal basin.3 John Morris and Thomas Lockwood had a considerable interest in the line; both were to be among the original shareholders in the Oystermouth Railway. It seems likely that plans to extend the line of communications from the Pottery into the town were the germ of the Oystermouth scheme. At a Corporation meeting of 8 August, 1800, it was revealed that Messrs. Lockwood had 'made a Waggon way over Corporation property near the Pottery' without permission, and it was resolved that they must pay rent. This may have been the first stage in linking the tramway with wharves nearer the town centre.4 Certainly when the Corporation authorized Henry Bonham's sub-letting of the brewery and its wharf to Samuel Hawkins in August, 1802, they laid down the condition 'of Mr. Bonham's permitting a railway or tramroad to be made to com-municate from the Bason of the Canal with the Bank of the Corporation in the possession of John Morris and others as of very great public utility and con-venience:5 In January 1803, the Duke of Beaufort sub-leased the northern part of Morris's bank (mentioned above) 'reserving to the Corporation sixty feet in depth from the Strand and the length of the bank for a public rail or tramroad or for extending the Canal and as far as the Corporation are empowered to grant it, that his Grace have permission to use the communication through the Brewery.' In February, 1803, the remainder of the bank was let to Gabriel Powell of Fairwood Lodge and to William Spencer on the same con-dition.7 It is significant that the names of Morris and the Duke of Beaufort were associated with developments at this early stage, and that the Corporation appeared favourable from the outset. Secondly, the possibility of a canal or 

tramroad was entertained as early as January, 1803. The Oystermouth Tramway as proposed in 1804, and as built, did include a branch from the Mount to the 2West Pier. In 1805 it was linked to 'Lockwood's Rail Road' near the brewery. The proprietors leased a wharf near the pier from the Corporation, later sub-leasing this to Lockwood and Morris severally.8 So the Oystermouth scheme developed out of plans for improving communications within the town. When, in July 1803, Edward Martin wrote to the Portreeve about 'a continuation of the [Swansea] Canal',9 the most likely explanation is that he was acting as agent and technical adviser to a group of promoters which included Morris, Lockwood and perhaps the Duke. Martin was a Morriston man, a colliery surveyor, canal and tramroad engineer, who played a large part in the construction of the subsequent railway and later became a shareholder. On 12 August, he addressed the burgesses on the subject of extending the canal to Mumbles, a destination now mentioned for the first time. The Corporation approved the plan in principle, asked Martin to make a survey, map and estimate, and opened a subscription to defray his expenses. The burgesses showed an awareness of the problems which were to arise by asking him to assess also 'the comparative advantages of a tram road as well through the whole line as partially through the town'." On 11 January, 1804, the Portreeve was authorized to subscribe £500 towards the canal scheme,11 and by 20 March, the Corporation was able to approve a printed copy of the Bill.1 2

The plan which accompanied the Bill was `taken by John Williams', a land surveyor, — presumably having been made at the time of Martin's survey. It is entitled `A Plan of the line of an intended Navigable Canal and a Railway or Tramroad from the Swansea Canal ' etc.1 3 Perhaps the branches to the West Pier and to the Clyne collieries were intended to be tramroads linking with the main Oystermouth Canal; this model, a canal linked to tramroad feeders, was a common one, and one to which Martin later reverted as engineer to the Penclawdd Canal and the Kidwelly & Llanelly Canal. He was apparently not attracted by the idea of long distance tramways, which had come into use notably in Gwent. In January, 1804, Swansea became the birthplace of Wales's first newspaper, the 

Cambrian, and from 18 February its pages , make a considerable contribution to our knowledge of events, for on that day criticisms of the Oystermouth Canal project were printed in a letter from one 'Spectator'. Martin answered in the following issue, and despite his hope that 'persons, having an objection to the intended measure, would not screen themselves under a feigned signature' the controversy was maintained until 7 April by correspondents styling themselves `Vindex', 'Speculator', 'A Reader', `Cincinnatus', `Octavius', 'A Constant Reader', `Meanwell', and 'Square Toes'. However, 'Spectator' and Martin remained the principals, and debated the two main points raised, namely, the threat of Mumbles becoming a port to rival Swansea, and the disadvantages of building a canal through the river wharves at Swansea. The first of these was best put by 'Spectator' in his first letter: "When completed, no doubt the clause empowering the Trustees of the Mumbles Light to build a Pier there, will be acted upon, and by that means a harbour sufficiently safe to permit the landing of vessels at Oystermouth will be formed a very large share of the present trade will be removed there, and no vessel will incur the additional port charges of the river and the attendant delays, unless she has a cargo inwards."14 At the time, the Swansea shippers were very con-scious of the commitments they were undertaking in respect of the new harbour Bill before Parliament. However, later scares about the growth of Mumbles were more realistic, when the development of steam railways might have made it possible for coal from the Dunvant Valley and further west to have been diverted 3away from Swansea's South Dock. In 1804, as Martin argued, it could `never be supposed by a rational person that coal worked on the Swansea river will be carried by the proposed Canal. through a good port to a much inferior one, at additional expense') 5 Certainly the provision of a deep water harbour at Mumbles would have been a very expensive business. The newspaper exchanges also illustrate the illusions of the promoters and their opponents. A Cambrian editorial of 18 February considered it self-evident that `on the line (were) inexhaustible quantities of coals and limestone of the best quality.' Martin reaffirmed an assurance he had made in September 1803 that the canal would mean Clyne coal in Swansea at 20 shillings per wey cheaper than Swansea Valley coal, and limestone at half the current price.1 6 Coal owners north of Swansea believed this boast, and opposed the canal, but it soon became apparent that it was an empty claim. John Morris's Clyne collieries never raised large tonnages, while a tramroad terminating near Oystermouth Castle did not even reach the major quarries of Mumbles Head. One perspicacious 'Reader' discerned this in 1804: regarding Clyne, he asked, `are there any coal works yet open from which any supply of coal is to be derived? ' and he considered limestone could be conveyed to Swansea more efficiently by expanding the existing fleet of lime boats and employing more quarrymen. He thought that, if a canal were built, a terminus at the West Pier would be quite adequate, and a junction with the Swansea Canal quite superfluous.' 7 Martin hoped a junction of the canals would facilitate transport of limestone from Oystermouth to the works at Landore, and of culm from the Tawe Valley to burn lime in Gower. This limited use of the lower reaches of the Swansea Canal was a worrying prospect for its proprietors, as we shall see. At a time when a journey from Swansea to Mumbles meant a walk or ride across the beach and, especially at night, the very real danger of drowning in a muddy pool, 1 8 the potential of a canal or railroad was naturally exaggerated — the industrial traffic, on the scale envisaged, never developed. The second point at issue was the contention that a canal intersecting the river-side wharves at the same level as the Swansea Canal would mean raising the ground level along the wharves, necessitating the use of expensive cranes to load ships, and thus raising costs at a time of important developments at the port. `Spectator' estimated a 10ft. 2in. fall from the level of the Swansea Canal-to high water mark) 9 `Square Toes' added that a road from Wind Street to the Burrows would have to be carried on a bridge 12ft. above the existing street level, that a canal would require an acre of town land, valued at £1,000, putting `a total stop to ship-building in any of the present situations between the Swansea Canal and the Mount' and sorely limiting warehouse space in the expanding port.2° 'Spectator's' solution was a tramroad through the wharves to a canal starting on the Burrows. Martin disputed his figures, and saw no need to build the new canal on the same level as the old, but his most interesting comments are on the tramroad suggestion. He dismisses the idea of a tramroad linking two canals — quite reasonably — as far too clumsy and expensive in transfer of goods, and concludes: 'It has always appeared to me that the whole line from Oystermouth to Swansea should be either a canal or a tramroad, and powers (as it is well known) are intended to be taken to carry either into effect, as may be most expedient: and I have no hesitation in declaring that if Mr. Trevithick's very ingenious machine is brought to that perfection, which some persons are confident it will be, and which, from the very liberal patronage it has received from Mr. Homfray of Pendarran (sic), there is every reason to hope for; that is, of driving waggons on a tramroad at a cheaper rate by 50 per cent than it can now be done by horses, 4that it will be most advantageous to the proprietors and the public to substitute an entire tramroad instead of a canal 2 1 The reference is to Trevithick's pioneering experiments with steam locomotives at Penydarren, described in the 

Cambrian in February in a 'Letter from Merthyr'. Martin was no doubt taken with the possibilities of locomotive traction, and this may have prompted the clause in the Bill which provided for 'haling or drawing' by 'men, horses or otherwise', phraseology which facilitated the use of steampower in 1877 without the passage of a further Act. Martin's first choice was a canal, but the tone of this passage shows he was by no means dogmatic. On 11 or 12 April, Martin met 'Spectator' on the canal bank to settle the question of water levels finally. This confrontation, though not its conclusions, is described in the Cambrian in a manner which shows that the puritanism of mid-Victorian England was still some years away: `A few days since, some ladies passing by the Swansea Canal, and observing several gentlemen assembled (who had met to ascertain the high water mark) enquired, with that curiosity natural to the sex, what they were about? to which an artless youth replied only: ladies, trying who can make most water'.2 2 The newspaper controversy had been notably lacking in personal invective, and there is some suggestion that the prinicipals had met and continued their argument. It is interesting that 'Square Toes' characterizes Martin as 'coal black', presumably the champion of the coal owners of the immediate environs of the town — Morris, Lockwood and the Duke — and 'Spectator' as 'light blue', perhaps the defender of the interests of the port.2 3 

One correspondent, `Meanwell', had proposed that differences be settled by a meeting of the people of Swansea. 2 

> 4

A meeting of the copper trade of the town had already resolved to resist the 'intended taxation involved in the new harbour Bill' before Parliament, cooperating with the-Swansea Canal Company in this.2 5 

The two Bills were linked in a Cambrian advertisement of the following week, which called a general meeting at the Bush on 26 March to ensure that neither measure injured 'the trade of Swansea and its Neighbourhood.' Among the signatories were Charles Smith the Llansamlet coal owner, George Haynes of the brewery and Lewis Weston Dillwyn of the pottery, all of whom might have had grounds for opposition, but also Charles Collins, a solicitor, and one of the original shareholders in the tramway. The Cambrian hoped the meeting would give the matter 'cool and dispassionate consideration' 26 

Colonel Warde of Woodlands (Clyne) Castle took the chair, declaring himself neutral, though this may be doubted.2 7 The meeting decided to appoint a committee to frame a petition to prevent the projected canal or tramroad becoming the basis of the growth of Mumbles as a port for export or import in competition with Swansea, and to avoid 'the ground along the West bank of the river, [being] ... intersected or in any way affected so as to incon-venience the port.. ' Among the signatories, apart from Smith, Haynes and Dillwyn, were Silvanus Padley, a prominent shipowner, Rees Jones, colliery agent to the impartial chairman, Thomas Sheasby, engineer to the Swansea Canal Company, as well as a group of Neath men who were proprietors of the Swansea Canal: Rees Williams of Aberpergwm, William Gwyn, R. G. Aubrey and J. N. Miers. Despite the doubts expressed, the aim of the meetinhseems to have been to insert safeguarding clauses into the Bill, not to block it. The Swansea Canal proprietors also called a Special General Assembly to organize their own petition to Parliament against the Oystermouth bill in its existing form. This took place on 16 April and was not reported. Among the signatories to the advertisement, all of whom were shareholders, six were 5colliery owners from the upper Tawe Valley: Rees Williams, Aubrey, William Shewen, Gronow, Gwyn and Jenkin Davies Berrington,2 9 (the last mentioned was also a Swansea solicitor). It can also be noted that Aubrey, Williams and Padley were to become Trustees under the 1804 Harbour Act. In the Library of the Royal Institution is a leaflet bearing a 'statement of facts' issued by the proprietors of the canal. While emphasizing that there was 'no desire to prevent the subscribers to the Oystermouth Canal from obtaining their Act', they wanted to add clauses forbidding use of the Swansea Canal except when it had a surplus of water, and of their wharves at all times. Since the majority of the canal's trade came from works and collieries well up the valley, the expected use of the first mile and a half, containing four locks, by Oyster-mouth Canal traders, would play havoc with water supplies, and hence reduce revenue. In conclusion, the document stressed that owners of works and collieries 'have expended very large capitals upon the Faith of Parliament, pledged to them by the Swansea Canal Act'. It seems quite likely this leaflet was compiled in connexion with attempts to lobby Parliament over the Oyster-mouth project.3 0 In following the Parliamentary fortunes of the Bill, the first impression one gains is that its opponents were nearly too late. On the same day as the Harbour Bill, 24 February, the Petition for leave to bring in a Bill for 'a Canal for the Navigation of boats, barges and other vessels, and a Railway or Tramroad for the passage of waggons and other carriages ' to supply Swansea and its environs with 'coal, limestone, and other articles at a much cheaper rate than at present' was presented to the Commons. Examination by committee began the following morning, and on 3 March the measure was reported as complying with standing orders. Incidentally, John Jeffreys, a Swansea solicitor and steward to the Duke of Beaufort, guided both Bills through Parliament: on 12 March both passed their first reading. On the 22nd the Oystermouth Bill was read a second time, and only after this did opposition arise. On 9 April, the Swansea Canal pro-prietors presented two petitions, protesting that both the harbour and canal measures would injure their interests and endanger the capital they had invested. The House referred the relevant petition to the committee considering the Oyster-mouth bill, and ordered that the canal proprietors' counsel be heard. No further opposition appeared until 8 May when two petitions were presented. One was from 'Owners of Wharfs, Quays, Docks, Houses, and other property in Swansea, or concerned in the trade there, or persons having lent money for the purpose of improving the Harbour of Swansea', demanding clauses protecting their interests. The second was in the names of J. N. Miers, S. F. Lettsom, John Wade, and J. R. Mander of the Ynispenllwch Tin Plate works and Iron Forges — they feared loss of water in the Swansea Canal would disadvantage them greatly. Both petitions were referred to the committe which was instructed to receive counsel from the petitioners, and also any replies the sponsors might give to the com-plaints. In the event, no additional representations were made by the last pet-itioners. On 23 May the committee reported that it had considered the various arguments, 'made several Amendments' and delivered the amended bill to the house. The spokesman for the committee was Francis Gregor, M.P. for Cornwall, who, at the first General Assembly of the Oystermouth Railway or Tramroad Company in July received the thanks of the proprietors for 'his able and zealous support in carrying through the different stages ... . '31 On 1 June, the House changed one of the amendments. On 5 June, the bill passed its third reading, and it was resolved 'that the Title be, An Act for making and maintaining a Railway or Tramroad ' Gregor took the Bill to the Lords, where it was read the first time on 5 June, the second time on the 6th, reported on the 11th. and read a 6third time on the 12th. It received the Royal Assent on 29 June.32 The pro-prietors paid John Jeffreys £159.11s. for his efforts, plus £320 expenses. Edward Martin also went to Westminster as an expert witness and received £65.33 Since copies of the 1804 Act have survived,34 it would be useful to compare them with the original Bill, to determine exactly how it was amended — but the author has been unable to find a copy of the Bill. Below are those phrases in the Act which were probably added, and the interests protected in them are too obvious for comment: `For every ton of coal or culm carried along the Railway and shipped at any place westward of the western pier of Swansea harbour, there shall be paid by the Company to the Trustees the sum of 5 shillings Construction must not interfere with 'the wharfs, banks and premises belonging to the Swansea Canal Company.' While up to 60 yards in width might be taken for construction anywhere else only 10 yards was permitted along the riverside. `No articles whatever [are to be] conveyed upon any part of the Swansea Canal, except when the water shall flow over the waste wier (sic.) upon the Morriston pond shall afterwards be conveyed along the Rail-way, under a penalty after the rate of 5 shillings per ton' — though this clause will only come into effect when the canal proprietors have built their own railway from Morriston pond to the Oystermouth Railway. One might hazard a guess that this last condition was the one imposed on an amendment on 1 June. The scheme of building a railway parallel to the canal was revived in the 1830S.35 To sum up, no opposition was expressed to the idea of improving communications between Swansea and Mumbles; this was generally considered a means of promoting prosperity. However, a number of local groups feared their interests would be affected by the scheme produced and, aroused rather belatedly by correspondence in their brand new newspaper, town meetings sponsored a Parliamentary lobby, which secured amendments in the measure, the major one being the substitution of a tramroad for a canal. 

REFERENCES 1. N. L. Thomas, Of Swansea West, The Mumbles Past and Present, (Gomer Press, 1978), p73. 

2. See 'A Plan of River Swansey in Glamorganshire, Taken A.D. 1771, by B. Jones' — reproduced in W. H. Jones, A History of the Port of Swansea,

8The Bexley Heath Railway 

Introduction The formation and building of the Bexley Heath Railway does not provide one of the highlights of railway history; indeed, it was one of the last lines to be constructed in North Kent. It is appropriate, therefore, that three of its `neighbour' lines, which were firmly established in this part of Kent, should be included in this essay. It is proposed to take these in order of construction. The London & Greenwich Railway In 1832 a 31/2-mile long railway was proposed between Greenwich and Tooley Street, London Bridge. About 2,000 people were moving daily over the 51/2-mile road between these two places and it was hoped to attract these as well as develop new traffic. The promoters adopted a scheme drawn up by a Lt.Col.G.T. Landmann; this was for a line carried on a brick viaduct of 878 arches. The first section of the L&GR, the first passenger and steam railway in London, was opened on 8 February 1836 from Spa Road, Bermondsey, to Deptford. Thus Spa Road became the first railway terminus in London, if only a temporary one, as this ceased on 14 December 1836 with the opening of the extension to the first London Bridge Station. There was a further extension from Deptford to Greenwich, opened on 24 December 1838. Principal Parliamentary Acts And Orders Incorporation of Company: construction of railway, 3-4 Wm.4. C.46. 1833; 7 Wm.4 & 1 Vic. C.50. 1837. Deptford Creek tolls, 7 Wm.4 & 1 Vic. C.120. 1837. Extension of time for railway: further powers, 1-2 Vic. C.4. 1838; 2-3 Vic. C.19. 1839: 3-4 Vic. C.127. 1840: 5-6 Vic. C.102. 1842: and 2 Ed.7.C.254. 1902. Construction of station in Southwark:, 3-4. Vic. C.128. 1840. Lease of railway to South Eastern Co: 8-9. Vic. C.80. 1845. The North Kent Railway North Kent was the scene of long and bitter battles dating back to 1845, which saw extensive but mutually destructive proposals not only by the South Eastern Railway Company but by the London & Croydon and by the London, Chatham & Dover and North Kent. In 1846 the SER obtained authority for the 221/4-mile North Kent Line, from North Kent East Junction via Lewisham, Blackheath and Dartford to Gravesend. Beyond that town it was to join the seven miles of line operated by the Gravesend & Rochester Railway and Canal Company, latterly the Thames & Medway Canal Company. The canal, opened in 1824, was built to save barges the longer route round the Isle of Grain. Between Higham and Strood two tunnels, now 1,531 and 2,329 yards long, separated by a 50-yard opening, which served as a passing place, were bored. On 10 February 1845 the canal company officially opened a single line railway along the towpath and on a stage erected over the water in the tunnels. In 1846 both canal and railway were purchased by the SER for £310,000. The canal in the tunnels was filled in and a double track laid throughout. North Kent trains began a through service between London Bridge and Rochester stations on 30 July 1849. In 1845 the SER had aquired, on lease, the London & Greenwich Railway but refusal by the Admiralty to agree on an extension of the Greenwich line, on grounds that the instruments of the Royal Observatory would be upset by the proximity of the trains, meant that when the North Kent line was authorized 9the junction was at North Kent East. Eventually, on 1 January 1873, an extension of the North Kent line was opened from Charlton to Maze Hill and finally, on 1 February 1878, from Maze Hill to Greenwich. Since 1876 there had been a connexion with the railway system of the Royal Woolwich Arsenal, at Plumstead, and also to the Royal Woolwich Dockyard. Consequently, during both World Wars, the North Kent line saw considerable traffic. During the First World War a station was built at Church Manor Way (between Plumstead and Abbey Wood) for the munition workers employed at the Arsenal. There were, and are now to a lesser degree, numerous other industrial branches on the North Kent, and between Dartford and Gravesend are paper mills and cement works. Further on, a large oil refinery has been constructed on the Isle of Grain. Principal Parliamentary Acts And Orders Widening of parts of the London & Greenwich Railway: 8-9. Vic. C.186. 1845; 10-11. Vic. C.230. 1847. Line to Gravesend and Woolwich: 9-10. Vic. C.305. 1846. Extensions at Greenwich and Woolwich: 28-29. Vic. C.243. 1865. 34-35. Vic. C.4. 1871. Gravesend & Rochester Change of name of Company of Proprietors of Thames & Medway Canal to Gravesend & Rochester Railway and Canal Company; maintenance of railway; 8-9. Vic. C.168. 1845. Purchase of railway and canal by the SER Co.: 9-10. Vic. C.339. 1846. The Dartford Loop Line To forestall any expansionist ideas from its rival, the London, Chatham & Dover Railway, the SER promoted, in 1862, a Bill dealing with the "Tunbridge and Dartford Lines". This Act constituted "Railway No. 1" (the New Main Line) which would begin at or near the junction between the North Kent and the Greenwich; and "Railway No. 2" (the Dartford Loop) which would begin at a point on the line of "No. 1" in the parish of Lewisham. The Act also stated that this line should be regarded as part of the North Kent Railway and could automatically charge tolls as if it were part of that railway originally. The line involved no engineering difficulties and was duly opened on 1 September 1866. At about this time Dartford Station was rebuilt and the embankment moved nearer to the mill pond of the Phoenix Paper Mills, (now Burroughs Wellcome), thus giving a Down Relief line and a third platform face. An entirely remodelled station was completed in 1973. With the advent of the First World War a munitions factory was opened by Vickers-Maxim just east of Crayford. To facilitate movement of special trains during the Second World War, a curve was opened on 11 October 1942 to com-plete the triangle at the junction of the Loop and the North Kent lines, west of Dartford. Principal Parliamentary Acts and Orders Tunbridge and Dartford lines etc.: 25-26. Vic. C.96.1862. The Bexley Heath Railway The genesis of the Bexley Heath Railway lay with a small group of local gentle-men who organized the first petition to the South Eastern Railway in 1881, for a line to Bexleyheath. The SER, after some delay, urged the petitioners to form their own company. With this decision the leader of the local party and 10 the probable instigator of the project, Squire Jones of East Wickham House, Welling, acted as Chairman to the committee of subscribers at their first formal meeting. At this meeting, Mr. Alfred W. Bean of Danson Park was elected Chairman, no doubt because of his past experience in railway construction. In association with his partner, Thomas Jackson of Eltham Park, he had been responsible for the building of many lines in Yorkshire and also the line from Welwyn to Hertford, nearer London. Capital for the venture was provided by local tradespeople, about one third of the initial capital being raised locally. Those involved were Colonel Barne, Mr. Charles Beadle, a coal and corn merchant (who was elected Vice-Chairman); Mr. Albert Hide, founder of Hide's Department Store; Mr. George Mence Smith, later to become founder of a chain of hardware stores; and Mr. G. E. Arnold, pastor of a chapel in Plumstead. Large sums were also provided by local landowners, such as Morgan Yeatman and Robert Kersey. The company's Solicitors were Messrs. Dolman & Pritchard of 3, Lawrence Pountney Hill, E. C. (the former being a local man of repute) at which the company transacted its business. Mr. Bean continued as Chairman until his death in July 1890. After a short period, in which Squire Jones held the position, A.W.T. Bean, the late Mr. Bean's son, took over his father's place. Among the railwaymen associated with the company, perhaps the most important was Mr. Francis Brady, then engineer of the SER, and the contractor for the line, Mr. Rigby of Calverton near Nottingham. In the early days of the company, the famous Sir Edward Watkin was still firmly entrenched as Chairman of the SER. By the late 1880s, however, the General Manager, Sir Myles Fenton, appears to have taken the largest proportion of the company's decisions. In the June of 1891 he became a Bexley Heath Director and two other SER men, Mr. Shaw and Mr. Sheath, became, at different times, secretaries, whilst a Mr. Skelton was an auditor. Thus the SER dominated the local company in the second half of its existence. In 1881 Bexleyheath, with its large detached houses and a respectable society, showed every sign of becoming a second Blackheath. Indeed, this is what was hoped by its inhabitants. The local council, with this in mind, ordained in 1894 that, henceforth, Bexley Heath should be written as one word to follow their ideal. The railway company was informed to this effect but when the station was opened its name appeared in two words. Even as late as 1954, whilst the platform name boards were correct, the canopy over the entrance had not been changed. With the formation of the Bexley Heath a long period of estrangement followed with the SER. This trouble arose after the SER had persuaded that company to make their western junction at Lee, on the Dartford Loop Line, instead of at Blackheath. Thus a Bill for the incorporation of the company to build a line from Crayford to Lee via Bexleyheath was submitted for the 1883 session. On 20 August 1883 this was given Royal Assent. Another period of differences arose, with the result that the western junction reverted to Blackheath. The amended Bill was given Royal Assent on 5 July 1887, despite Sir Myles Fenton's misgivings. The map shows three lines — that to Lee, the original plan in 1883; that to Blackheath, considered the best by the SER General Manager in 1884; and that to Blackheath as actually constructed. 11 Apart from the internal battles, the main external trouble was over the way the railway would cross Mr. Cator's land at Blackheath Park. Eventually a tunnel was constructed. The contract for the construction of a double track, standard gauge line, was finally awarded to Mr. Rigby in the summer of 1890, work starting in August 1891. The line was to be opened in 1894, but owing to an embankment slip at Blackheath it was postponed until 1 May 1895. Constructional Details The Bexleyheath line deviates from the North Kent Line at Blackheath Junction on a sharp curve of 13 chains radius, where, on the right of the line a concrete retaining wall was constructed to avoid taking part of Colonel McNeill's back garden. On the right hand side and still evident is the site of the earth slip of 1894. The line passes on through the tunnel of the Cator dispute to reach Kidbrooke Station, built in order that the Earl of St. Germains could develop his land. This materialized only recently. This station, until 1973, was the only one on the line to retain its original wooden buildings. Passing on, Eltham (Well Hall), formally Well Hall (see table) is reached. This station is approached by a sharp curve of 12 chains radius, which was necessitated by the change of the proposed line of the railway. In the long cutting between here and Welling are situated the next two stations of more recent construction — Eltham Park (see table) opened in 1908 for the first class season ticket holders in the early days of the select Eltham Park Estate, hence its palatial appearance; then Falconwood, opened in 1936 for the newly-constructed housing estate of the same name. A long embankment then leads on to Welling Station. Passing on, Bexleyheath is reached. The original plan was to build the station with its goods sidings on the west side of Brampton Road, on land owned by Sir Julian Goldsmid, but with the intervention of Robert Kersey, owner of the land on the east side of Pickford Lane, the station was constructed here instead. The line continues on to the last station on the line, Barnehurst, so named after the owner of the land, Colonel Barne and hurst to commemorate the station's woodland situation. After leaving this station the line falls on a long embankment down to the marshes where it rejoins the North Kent Line at Crayford Creek Junction.. Later Developments The Bexley Heath Railway Company was an independant entity in name only as it was sponsored and worked by the SER and so it was that in 1900 the Company was dissolved and transferred to the SER, although more correctly, by then, the South Eastern & Chatham Railway Company. At the time of the formation of the Southern Railway in 1923, electrification became a priority. Hitherto services had been entirely operated by steam traction. The standard third rail electrification was adopted and services began on the Charing Cross and Cannon Street to Dartford (via Greenwich, Blackheath, Bexleyheath and Sidcup) routes on 19 July 1926, although being advertised to start on the 12th. A restricted service was operated for a short while from 6 June. Services from Dartford to Gravesend started on 6 July 1930. The locomotive depot, in steam days, for the suburban services was at Slade[s] Green but with electrification this was converted to an electric carriage and repair depot. Through services to the Kent Coast, special trains and goods services continued to be steam operated, the main depots being at Bricklayers Arms and Hither Green. With Phase 1 of the Kent Coast electrification in 1959 steam traction faded until finally, in 1961, it disappeared altogether. 12 In 1935, passenger traffic was able to use a connexion which had been made from Lewisham to the Greenwich Park branch line. This had not been used since 1917 and the connexion enabled trains to run to Blackfriars and Holborn Viaduct Stations. This made it unnecessary to pass through London Bridge and the Union Street Spur. With regard to the stations, Kidbrooke, as previously mentioned, was the least changed of the original stations until recently. The station footbridge was added in the early 1950s, Eltham (Well Hall), Welling and Bexleyheath getting their footbridges when the line was electrified and the accomodation on the "Up" side rebuilt in 1932. It is, however, only over the past few years that considerable change has been seen. Several of the stations have received 'bus-stop' type shelters and rationalization has meant the closure of the goods yards, apart from Kidbrooke. By 1955 all of the platforms had been extended to accommodate 10-car trains. On 1 October 1970 a new signal box became operative at Dartford. Controlling most of the Greenwich and North Kent Lines, the Bexleyheath and the Dartford Loop Lines, this has meant the closure of the older signal boxes, the abolition of semaphore signalling and the introduction of full colour light signal-ling. In 1949, in order to try and solve the increasing passenger problem, two four-car double-deck electric units were introduced. These were not a full deck above, as the bridge heights restricted this, but intersecting decks. They did not prove a great success and up until their withdrawal in 1971 were limited to a few peak hour services. The very nature of the line has made it unsuitable for fast through trains, there-fore all East Kent traffic uses the North Kent Line via Greenwich. Accidents It is only recently that serious accidents marred the record of the Bexleyheath Line. Previously, mishaps were the occasional derailed coal truck, or in very wet weather, an earth slip, but on 11 June 1972 a serious derailment occurred at Eltham (Well Hall) Station. The train involved was a London Midland Region staff excursion returning from Margate and was made up of LMR stock hauled by a Class 47 locomotive No. 1630. As this was a cross-London transfer working Hither Green Depot provided the crew for the journey over the Southern Region and the return working was via the Bexleyheath Line. At the station the loco-motive took the 12 chain curve at more than the 20 m.p.h. restriction, jumped the track and ploughed across the former goods yard. In the wreckage six people, including the driver, died and 126 were injured. The enquiry on the accident established that the driver had impaired his ability to drive by over-drinking and had entered the curve at about 65 m.p.h. The second man in the cab survived the accident but he had no memories immediately prior to the derailment. The Future The coming of the railway to North Kent and the ultimate electrification of the system has been, no doubt, the main cause of the population explosion in this area. Over recent years the problem of conveying passengers to and from London has increased, despite the movement of factories and a decline in the population away from Central London. Services have nearly reached saturation point, and several suggestions have been made to try and alleviate this problem: extending the Jubilee Line of London Transport to Docklands, then beyond to Woolwich and Thamesmead, or to take the Bexleyheath line into the London Transport system. The line today is only a small part of a highly integrated and important system — a far cry from 1895. 13 Principal Parliamentary Acts And Orders Incorporation of company; construction of railway etc; 46-47. # Some Doubts on Primary Sources 

BY JOHN DENTON The importance of using primary sources, especially company minutes, has long been accepted by transport historians. But experience in a field somewhat remote from the transport scene has cast — for me at least — considerable doubts on the reliability of the company minute book. What does it tell us? It is supposed to be an account of what was discussed and decided at meetings. But is it? For over two years, I was until recently Administrative Officer to a national organization. An important function of this organization was to take evidence from numerous bodies and individuals, to try to assess its worth and then to act as a catalyst between them on the one hand and Government and local authorities, etc. on the other. I was required to act as Secretary to the Council at its quarterly Executive meetings and minute the proceedings. It was at these meetings lasting five hours or more that the main decisions were taken — decisions that could often have far reaching effects within the Principality of Wales. Partly in a form of shorthand, I often covered at least a dozen large sheets with notes in less than five hours. Back at the office afterwards, these would be drastically condensed to about two sheets of foolscap for the published minutes — yet even my first draft taken during the meeting would only contain a fraction of what was discussed and aired by the members and delegates. I tried very hard to make my minutes an accurate account of what went on at those meetings, yet it must be admitted that with the best will in the world, they were still my personal condensation of what I believed had taken place. Of course the minutes had to be approved at the next meeting three months later. Invariably they were so without amendment. That is hardly surprising for I had taken more comprehensive notes than anyone else present. I had no axe to grind and had no vested interest in anything — yet I know it would be quite wrong to claim that my minutes were an accurate record of the proceedings. Even resolutions sometimes had to be altered when it was noted that the wording actually agreed by the meeting had either a logical or grammatical flaw which would make them unworkable. 15 In the light of this it is surely reasonable to assume that the minutes of many a railway or canal company were still more inaccurate as a record of what went on. It is hardly necessary to try to catalogue the reasons for this. Anyone who has studied a railway company minute book — or published minutes (which are not the same thing) — will have noted the odd outburst of dissent from a shareholder in which his 'demolition' by the Chairman is given far more prominence. How much else was said that went unrecorded? Are we able to judge the true position? Yes, of course the minute books should be studied, but let us stop treating them as gospels. They are not. Perhaps worse is the excessive emphasis on contemporary newspapers. Agreed they too should be consulted, but only on the understanding that their accuracy is often grossly at fault. In the days when typesetting was still done by hand, the newspaper was just as anxious as now to rush into print with its stories before a rival got there first — and frequently before the facts could be verified. Read a series of different newspaper accounts of a major railway accident and later compare them with the official report of the subsequent inquiry and note how much they are at variance with each other and with the findings. I know which evidence I would be more ready to accept. The word 'contemporary' is not an automatic label for reliability as some members of the primary source school would have us believe. By that token Victorian engineers should only be read in Smiles and not in Rolt. When the late and much lamented L.T.C. Rolt wrote some of his biographies, he surely did not need further contemporary evidence to see that Smiles had certain typical Victorian hobby-horses which biased his accounts. Using his intelligence and viewing the scene from afar, he was able to see the wood for the trees. Interesting though it is to read Smiles, who wrote a contemporary account, I prefer to rely on Rolt's interpretations, written a hundred years afterwards. But if this makes us wary of what we are trained to regard as the only reliable sources, we can take heart in new avenues of acceptability: 'Never take notice of the ramblings of the oldest inhabitant' was good advice and should still be heeded if there is no way of measuring them. In the past decade, however, oral history has taken on a new meaning with the excellent work done by an increas-ing number of individuals and bodies concerned with obtaining accurate and reliable information by this means — and much of it is information that is not available in primary source material. A study of the books of George Ewart Evans or Paul Thompson's 'The Voice of the Past' (O.U.P. 1978) will reveal that a great deal of research has been done recently on the reliability one can place on various types of oral evidence and methods of obtaining it. It is achieving the status of a new science and properly applied will open up new fields to the historian. By all means let us continue to place high emphasis on primary source material, but let us be aware of its pitfalls. At the same time let us accept that there are other sources of reliable information — and to get the story right we need all the information we can obtain. 16 Witham Navigation Improvement

GENTLEMEN, As the City of Lincoln must be very materially interested in the important propositions for Improving the Drainage of the Country bordering on the River Witham and its collateral Branches, and the Navigation of the said River, but most particularly in the latter, and as you have done me the honor of asking my Opinion as to the proportionate degree of benefit which may be derived to the City of Lincoln and to the adjoining Country interested in the improvement of the Navigation, if carried into effect as proposed by the Bill now before Parliament, I shall endeavour to submit my Opinion with strict impartiality. In the first place it appears to me that the Scheme proposed by Mr. Rennie is likely to effect the purpose of Complete Drainage, but as it is understood that half of the Expence is to be provided for by an Augmentation of the Tolls on the Navigation, I think the improvement of the Navigation, as proposed by the Bill in its present form, falls considerably short of what might be reasonably expected by those more interested in the Navigation than in the Drainage. As it appears to be essentially necessary for the Drainage, it is already proposed by Mr. Rennie that from Boston to next Stixwould Ferry, a length of about eighteen Miles, the depth of the River shall be nine feet under the surface of the Water as kept up by the Gage at the Great Sluice at Boston, and that the bottom Width shall be from 50 feet to 33 Feet 6 Inches, which is amply sufficient for Sea Vessels of Eighty Tons burthen; but from this point upwards to Stamp End Lock, which is 14 Miles further, or nearly 32 Miles from Boston, the bottom width will decrease from 33 Feet 6 Inches to 28 Feet. An Increase in the width of this latter 14 Miles to 33 Feet 6 Inches, so as to make it sufficient for such Vessels to Stamp End Lock, which is within 31/2 Furlongs of the High Bridge at Lincoln, would cost about £5000. As it is obvious that such a Navigation would be highly beneficial to the Country at large and particularly to the Capital of the County, it can hardly be supposed that so small an Addition of Expence, to what would without it be necessary for the purposes of Drainage, would for a Moment be objected to. But as the Title of the Bill has naturally led to the Expectation that the restoring and improving the Navigation shall extend between the High Bridge at Lincoln and the Sea, the mode of effecting this, or something adequate to this intention, demands a more serious consideration. # The Junction point of the Trent and Trent & Mersey Canal 

BY JOHN E.HEATH The vagueness of the terminal points of canals in the acts of authorization makes it difficult to ascertain the exact line of the waterway and therefore it might be assumed that the line of the canal was in the hands of the engineer. In the case of the Trent & Mersey Canal, this vagueness is shown at its western end where it was to join the River Mersey 'at or near a certain place called Runcorn Gap .... This was clarified by the Duke of Bridgwater in a petition to the House of Commons on 12 March 1766 in which he argued that the Trent & Mersey Canal, instead of terminating as planned 'at or near the Runcorn Gap', should link with the Duke's canal 'at or near a Brook, called Preston Brook, near Preston', the Duke undertaking to provide the link from Preston Brook to Runcorn Gap. In the initial petition for the Trent & Mersey Canal (15 January 1766) there is a similar vagueness about the eastern starting point. It was proposed that the canal should start 'from the River Trent, at or near Wilden Ferry ' , and Wilden Ferry was retained in the Third Reading of the Bill (12 April 1766) when it was passed to the House of Lords. Dr. Jean Lindsay, in her book The Trent and Mersey Canal (1979), writes that the preamble to the Act was the same as that in the First Petition except that instead of Wilden Ferry, 'near Wilden Bridge' is used. It is worth pointing out that Wilden Ferry was a significant point on the River Trent Navigation. The ferryman at the time, and some one hundred or more years previous, controlled the navigation upstream of that point to King's Mills and downstream to Nottingham. It would seem to be natural, therefore, to take the canal into the Trent at a point near the Ferry, the ferryman, a Leonard Fosbrooke, controlling the traffic from that point onward, as the Duke of Bridgwater controlled the traffic at the Mersey end. This may account for the Trent & Mersey Canal coming to a point within ten or so yards of the River Trent, upstream of Wilden Ferry at a point where there was a wooden warehouse (Sutton Papers, Derby Record Office) between the Loughborough to Derby Turnpike Road and the River Trent (see Map). It is possible that it was Brindley's original plan to lock down into the Trent by at least one more and possibly two locks at the present site of the No. 2 lock, Shardlow, as is the case at Stourport. In fact the canal continues eastward across the flat landscape descending by a lock to a level where it can join the River Trent at its confluence with the River Derwent (Derwentmouth) some 2000 yards downstream from Wilden Ferry. In the period between the publication of the initial survey of the line of the canal in 1758 and the passing of the Act, the Loughborough to Derby Turnpike Trust, in February 1758, decided to replace the Ferry at Wilden with a bridge, the construction of which appears to have taken place between July 1758 and 1761 when it was opened to traffic. This was the bridge referred to in the Act as Wilden Bridge and soon to be called Cavendish Bridge, after its major sponsor. The bridge had two arches and a central pier, and the pier was an obstruction to the passage of boatmen using the river. These belligerent boatmen had to be reminded by John Hope, who was Clerk to the Trustees of the Bridge, that action would be taken against them:— 'Great damage lately done by Watermen wilfully driving their boats against piles belonging to the bridge now building at Wilden Ferry .... ' (Derby Mercury 31 August 1 758). 

Is it possible that this obstruction to navigation created by the building of the bridge made Brindley change the line of the canal in order to avoid it? It is worth noting that the milestones along the line of the canal, which are referred to in the third reading of the Bill, commence at Shardlow and not at Derwentmouth, thereby depriving the Trent & Mersey Canal of about 1860 yards of waterway. A final thought: if the canal had entered the River Trent above Wilden Ferry, then the Wilden marked on the map in Jean Lindsay's book might have been a reality, instead of Shardlow! 19 Correspondence

NEIL PITTS Sir, — I have also been mystified by the connecting link between the Rhondda & Swansea Bay Railway at Pontrhydyfen and the South Wales Mineral Railway east of Gyfylchi Tunnel mentioned in David Garnett's letter. Neither the SWMR Working timetable of March 1918 nor that of the Port Talbot Railway of July 1914 (which includes, of course, the SWMR between Tonmawr and Glyncorrwg) makes any mention of it. The R&SB WTT lists no trains booked to work over it, nor does it appear in lists of gradients or double- and single-line sections. In fact it is only referred to under the list of engine whistle codes! Reference in the SWMR minute books is made on 14 July 1896 to letters passing between the two companies on the subject of the No. 8 railway although details of the contents are not given. It is clear that the SWMR opposed con-struction of the line as on 16 February 1897 a petition against the R&SB Bill of 1897 (for Revival of Powers in respect of Railway No. 8) was approved. On 13 July the failure of this opposition was reported. The SWMR Board considered terms to be asked of the R&SB for the junction easement on 2 November 1897 On 5 April 1898 the plan of the junction received their approval. Then on 19 July a copy of a memorandum between the two companies 'as to the Rhondda Company entering on the land' was presented and the price to be asked for the junction easement was again considered together with the question of a royalty on traffic diverted at the junction. Thereafter the minute books are silent on the subject until 15 February 1909. (In the meantime, of course, the Port Talbot had taken over the working and management of the SWMR from the Glyncorrwg Colliery Company Ltd., on 1 January 1908). The manager Mr. Lowther reported 'that he had arranged with the R&SB Company that the form of easement to be given by the SWMR in connexion with this junction should include in it an arrangement that the R&SB shall not open their junction for coal traffic so long as the SWMR shall not attempt to cross from their railway over the River Avon to the opposite side of the Avon Valley to divert coal traffic now served by the R&SB and that the coal traffic shall continue to be dealt with as at present, viz.: via the PT Railway or 20 the Briton Ferry incline as the SWMR and PTR may mutually agree." This Grant of Easement was approved and sealed on 19 July 1909 to be replaced apparently by two documents approved and sealed on 20 October, one dealing with the Grant of Easement only, the other dealing with the boundaries at the junction. All of this is a bit vague and gives no real indication of why the line was opened, what traffic it was meant to carry and if, indeed, it ever did carry any. Does the wording of the minute of 15 February 1909 imply that the R&SB constructed this length of line merely as a threat to the SWMR and an insurance against the SWMR and PTR poaching traffic from the pits along the southern bank of the Avon? It seems unlikely that the R&SB would expect to siphon much traffic off the SWMR since the majority of collieries to the east of the junction were in the hands of the Glyncorrwg Colliery Company, who operated the SWMR anyway. Of course, after 1908, when the line passed out out of their hands they might look elsewhere for an outlet for their traffic. Perhaps the R&SB minute books might offer some more clues to this intriguing problem. J. A. PEDEN 

Kilsby Tunnel 

Sir, — Since reading Mr. Clinker's comments on the date of the opening of the London & Birmingham Railway, I have looked through several contemporary local papers over the period concerned in search of evidence on the subject, and have found the following: 

Lincoln & Stamford Mercury 6.4.1838: Company advt. 'The public are informed that from and after Monday the 9th of April the Railway will be open for the conveyance of passengers between London and Birmingham'. There is no mention of any coach link, but in the next week Derby Mercury 

11.4.1838: 'The Railway Company have engaged 20 coaches, employing 700 horses, to convey passengers between Denbigh Hall and Rugby on the opening of the Railway On Monday morning [9th] a further portion [from Tring] to Denbigh Hall was opened At the other end of the line, a dis-tance of 30 miles has been opened from Birmingham to Rugby.' 

Derby Mercury 20.6.1838: Company Advt. 'The public are informed that on Sunday the 24th June and on every succeeding Sunday until further notice the train which now leaves London at 91/2 a.m. for Denbigh Hall will run to Birmingham, and an additional train will leave Birmingham at 10 a.m. for London, stopping at all stations.' (As in April, no mention is made of any coach link, but what follows seems to make it absolutely clear that this continued, for this train also, between Denbigh Hall and Rugby.) 

Derby Mercury 27.6.1838: 'It is intended to open the railway up to Roade on Monday [2nd July] , but only for passengers coming to Northampton and the eastern part of the country. Passengers travelling from London to Birmingham will go as at the present time, viz. from Denbigh Hall to Rugby by coach or omnibus.' 

Derby Mercury 25.7.1838: 'Marshal Soult left London at 1/2 past 4 in the morn-ing by the Birmingham Railway. The directors conveyed his Excellency to Liverpool, including the posting from Denbigh Hall to Rugby, in ten hours.' (This does not mention how the baggage was conveyed, but it seems clear that the railway was not yet considered fit to carry the Marshal's party throughout.) 

Nottingham Review 27.7.1838: 'On Wednesday morning [probably 18th, per-haps 25th] a number of engineers and director of the L&B Railroad made an experimental journey from Denbigh Hall as far as the town of Kilsby The journey was made for the purpose of testing the stability of the road.' 21 Derby Mercury 22.8.1838 (quoting Liverpool Albion): 'An engine and train, with some of the directors, will leave Birmingham at 7 a.m. on Monday next, the 20th., for London, being the first train that will pass over the entire length of the railway.' (If 'the first train carrying passengers' is intended, this does not preclude the passing of Marshal Soult's baggage, but it does deny the passing of any public passenger train as early as 24th June.) 

Nottingham & Newark Mercury 25.8.1838: Directors' Report at General Meeting. 'A single line of rails is laid, over which a train has already passed with several of the Proprietors, from end to end, the first excursion along the entire line to London The directors commenced booking passengers for the whole distance between London & Birmingham on 9th April. ' (Again, this does not preclude the passage of a baggage-train). 

Lincoln & Stamford Mercury 21.9.1838: Company Advt. 'The Public are informed that on and after Monday the 17th September the railway will be opened for the conveyance of passengers and parcels, private carriages and horses, throughout the whole distance between London and Birmingham.' 

Nottingham & Newark Mercury 22.9.1838: 'The first train, which arrived in Birmingham at 9.45 a.m. was the first train for the conveyance of passengers that ever passed through the celebrated Kilsby Tunnel.' (Again, the first public pass-enger train.) All this seems to make it clear beyond reasonable doubt that the sequence of events was: 9.4.1838 Public opening to Denbigh Hall and from Rugby to Birmingham. Through bookings between London and Birmingham. 24.6.1838 An additional Sunday train over these sections, but continuing the coach-link, even with this train. 28.6.1838 Laying of last brick in Kilsby Tunnel. 2.7.1838 Public opening (for Northampton traffic only) from Denbigh Hall to Roade. Birmingham traffic as before. 18.7.1838 A party travelled as far as Kilsby Town. 20.7.1838 Marshal Soult's baggage may have traversed the whole line. 20.8.1838 Directors' special train traversed the whole line. 17.9.1838 Public opening throughout for regular passenger traffic. G. Y. HEMINGWAY 

Staggered Platforms 

Sir, — The observations of Dr. Course are most welcome, and appear to confirm that there is a problem in explaining this particular layout. Regarding passenger safety, if we assume the conventional stagger, i.e. platforms 'downstream' of a level crossing, passengers alighting from a train and about to cross the line would be masked by the last vehicle of their train. But if one were due on the other line, and the staff were efficient, the gates would be closed across the road, and they would be safe provided they did not walk off the end of the platform to bypass the gates (one might expect to find that the platform ends adjacent to the cross-ing would not be sloped in the usual manner, and would be fenced, to discourage this obvious temptation). Regarding concern for road traffic, Lewin (Early British Railways p. 130) says of the Board of Trade Railway Department's second report (1842) 'As serious acci-22 dents had occurred by collision with road vehicles at level crossings the department gave special attention to the question.... A short Act passed in 1839, supplementary to the Highways Act of 1835, enjoined upon all railway companies the duty of providing proper gates and stationing gatekeepers at all crossings of public roads.. ..but the question as to whether the gates should nor-mally stand across the road or across the railway needed definite settlement.' The Acts for the earlier companies stated that the gates should be closed against the railway, except for the passing of trains, 'apparently under the misapprehen-sion that protection was thereby afforded to road passengers.' The department pointed out the absurdity of this assumption and recommended that in future the normal position of gates be across public highways, and this provision was included in the Regulation of Railways Act of 1842. The concern was for the safety, rather than the convenience of road users, and the provision was no doubt more inconvenient for them, since it is a fair assumption that in these early years the combined number of carts, coaches, pedestrians, horsemen and cattle would be generally greater than the number of trains. All this is worth bearing in mind, as staggered platforms seem often to have been associated with level crossings. It would be interesting to know if examples of staggering occur on single lines, at stations with passing loops (although this would clearly be avoided on the grounds of extra track expense unless overriding considerations existed), and in general if anyone can add to Dr. Course's examples of responses to site conditions — in the case of the Louthton line stations there were originally no sizings to condition the layout. The collection of more data on the subject seems desirable, and the following examples have come to the writer's notice. Mr. Borley advises New Southgate GNR — conventional arrangement, level crossing apparently between the platform ends; also Hatfield, GNR. , conventional, but level crossing was at the north end of the down platform. There were examples on the Grimsby — Louth line, GNR (see Railway Magazine April 1980 p. 173, no details). Mr. J. Brooks advises Welton, LNWR., conventional, overbridge between the platforms may have orig-inally been a level crossing. Berkswell LNWR., conventional, with level crossing, and Barnt Green, MR., conventional, position of level crossing, if any, not known, are both noted and illustrated in Clinker: Railways of the West Midlands; A Chronology, 1808 — 1954. Both were later rebuilt with parallel platforms. Mr. J. E. Norris advises Newland Halt, GWR, between Worcester and Malvern, con-ventional, opened in 1929. A colleague, Mr. P. Asquith, advises me that Boldon Colliery (originally Brockley Whins, in Durham) had staggered platforms conventionally about a level crossing with a lane, and that it was firmly held locally that the arrangement was used to take advantage of the crossing facility offered by the lane, to save the expense of, for example, a footbridge. But why the platforms had to be staggered to achieve this purpose is not clear — perhaps the siting alone was thus attributed. I believe also that Heighington S&D also had staggered platforms at the time of the Society's visit in 1975. H. W. PAAR Sir, — A paper 'On the Arrangement and Construction of Railway Stations', read before the Institution of Civil Engineers on 27 April 1858 by Robert Jacomb Hood, refers to this practice. Jacomb Hood was engineer of the London, Brighton & South Coast Railway, so that his statements can be regarded as pretty authoritative. He says that staggered platforms were adopted 'where no footbridge over or under is provided' to facilitate crossing the line when two trains arrived at the station at the same time, `so that a clear space can always be maintained between the ends of the two trains, when standing at the platforms.' 23 He adds that this arrangement also 'offers many facilities for connecting sidings with the main lines, and with one another.' G. MARTIN SMITH
