Sir, — I was interested in this article as I had already read the book and had just come back from a short holiday in Folkestone. While there I bought a book called Folkestone — the Story of a Town by C. H. Bishop. The author devotes pages 84 to 96 to the harbour and goes into a lot of detail of how the harbour was bought by the SER for £18,000 in 1843. The railway they were building was about a mile inland from the harbour, and so W. Cubitt had to incorporate the harbour in his plans. His solution was to build a junction and a station at the east end of the viaduct, and a subsidiary line known as the 'Tram Road' was built in 1843 to connect with the harbour. Incidentally, the road down to the harbour past this line is still called 'Tram Road' today. At first the line was regarded only as a means of carrying coal from the harbour to Coking Sheds near the [present] East station, and the SER intended to use Folkestone as its chief source of coke for all its locos. The first cross-channel service was on 1 August 1843, the railway being opened to Folkestone on 28 June of that year; they also built the Pavilion Hotel by the harbour in 1843. Between 1843 and 1849 boat passengers had to alight at the Junction Station and walk to the harbour or take the ramshackle horse bus down the steep streets. Charles Dickens, who visited Folkestone in the early days (he stayed at the British Lion, which still exists and has a Dickens room), had some amusing comments upon the hardship of the first travellers in his article 'Out of Town' which he wrote for his Household Words. To avoid these discomforts the SER sought powers to convey passengers down the branch line of the Tram Road and the first swing bridge was built in 1849, and a new station was built on the foreshore beyond the South Quay, and so by accident Folkestone got a station actually in the town, and for many years this was the most popular point of departure. A. T. WARWICK

Neglected Lines of Research 

Sir, — I am aware that this note may merely reveal the depth of my own ignorance. I can claim only two justifications for it. I have access to a very extensive library of waterways material; and my job brings me into contact with students who are setting out to retread old ground in their dissertations, rather than cultivate the new. Studies have been published of individual waterways; I know that additional studies are in progress or await a publisher. One looks in vain for much infor-mation on the Weaver, the Leeds & Liverpool or the Bridgwater & Taunton. Much neglected is the relation of agriculture and waterways. The index to Nigel Harvey's recent Industrial Archaeology of Farming in England & Wales gives one reference to canals. We learn that canals made slates available for the construc-tion of farm buildings! For some canals, e.g. the Bude, farms were the primary customer. For many others, agriculture provided a considerable traffic. How was the trade organized from isolated rural wharfs: how large were their catch-ments? Surely this is an aspect which demands investigation. Lime and waterways had a symbiotic relationship, and the new availability of lime was vastly important to the development of agriculture. What was the structure of the waterside lime-burning industry? It was perhaps an odd one, with Froghall and Bugsworth co-existing with many small and dispersed units. We seem to know little about the provisioning and logistics of canal construction. Suddenly a host of navvies descended on a country district. They needed food and much drink. They needed timber and bricks. They needed great numbers of thorn quicks for hedge-planting. There are enigmas here. The local economy could not, one supposes, supply all these sudden requirements. For the Stroudwater, Michael Handford has provided some tantalizing hints of the prob-lem. One nurseryman's accounts show a sudden demand for quicks. The Brick Tax operated during much of the major period of canal construction so one would expect many canal structures to be made of 'large' bricks; or did the canal companies manage to evade the tax? 25 Did canals play no part in smuggling? With wool a substantial item in the 'free trade' it is difficult to believe that the Owlers did not use the waterways to move such a bulky commodity. (We know from Harry Hanson's Canal Boatmen that other forms of roguery were well organized). Finally, the pubs. We know they were a vital element in the canal economy, but we seem to lack facts about their role and operation. I suspect that a weakness of waterways research is that it is too isolated, inad-equately inter-disciplinary. And that is probably a reflection of a lack of insti-tutional interest and funding. (Of 258 projects listed in the 1978 Register of Countryside Research, only five relate to canals — other than projects being undertaken within BWB). PHILIP DANIELL 

Fireless Steam Tugs 

Sir, — D. Gordon Tucker's interesting contribution to the November .journal 

prompts me to ask whether there is any evidence that the Mekarski compressed air system was ever tried for the same purpose. It was contemporary with Lamm and Francq's fireless system, actually pre-dating it as a proven alternative to con-ventional steam power on tramways. It was more widely applied and lasted much longer, the last Mekarski trams running in Nantes as late as April 1918. Indeed, it is seldom realized that the compressed air locomotive was always more numer-ous than its fireless contemporary right to the end of construction of both types in the 1960s. Becuase most twentieth century air locomotives worked under-ground, however, the type is virtually unknown to the average enthusiast. The Mekarski system was fairly complex, hut had certain advantages over the fireless one, particularly in respect of energy storage per unit weight. There are some strange inconsistencies in the figures quoted by Mr. Tucker. The performance of the tugs in regular service fell far short of the outputs quoted on p. 84. Taking the total run of 9km stated to be performed on one charge of stored energy, this would have taken 5 hours 51 minutes at the speeds given in the table of dimensions. The total energy storage was only 82hp-hr, so the aver-age output cannot have been more than 14hp. Moreover, this is quoted as a brake output, i.e. at the engine coupling, and thus the output on the towrope must be lower by the amount lost in friction and in pushing the tug itself through the water, the latter being no small amount in the confined waterway of a tunnel. Thus the net output on the rope cannot have exceeded 9hp or thereabouts. I suggest that the 16-17hp quoted on p. 84 is the maximum achieved on trial, with the engine producing its full 28bhp at 50rpm, and cannot represent normal prac-tice as the powerplant could not possibly sustain this effort for more than 2'/2hr or thereabouts. The design was curious in more than one respect. The engine specification was ludicrous, for one thing. It was a compound, yet the working pressure was a mere 56psig. One might think it was fitted with a condenser, so that it exhausted down to something like 3 psia (24in vacuum), in which case compounding would make sense, but the performance figures suggest otherwise. A compound working across a pressure ratio of 20:1 should be more efficient than a simple engine taking steam at the same pressure and exhausting to atmosphere, and a loco-motive charged to an initial pressure of 240psig should be able to store more energy per unit mass of water than one charged at 160psig anyway. Yet Francq's compound tug engine achieved nothing better than one horsepower-hour for every 401 lb water in the receiver. By comparison, an early Borsig fireless indus-trial working at 160psig (reduced to 40psig), simple, non-condensing, required only 380 lb of water per stored horsepower-hour. The inference is that the Francq tugs were not fitted with condensers that achieved any appreciable vac-26 uum and that the extra storage capacity afforded by the higher working pressure cancelled out the inefficiency of using a compound engine when a simple one would have sufficed. Some form of condenser doubtless was fitted, but only to prevent the emission of exhaust steam in the tunnel. The engine seems to have had yet another defect, that of running at a ridicul-ously low speed. As the engine was geared directly to the traction chain, the lower haulage speed in the tunnel could only be achieved by running the engine slower, so the in-tunnel speed was no higher than 30 rpm, giving a piston speed of only 79ft/min. It is little wonder that it was rather inefficient; a more enlightened design might have increased the energy storage by 50%. Francq and Mesnard were not alone, however, in believing that a compound engine was inherently more efficient than a simple, regardless of working pressure; it was a common delusion then, and later. Their last creation was rather more impressive — the large fireless 2-6-2 tanks built for the petite ceinture in Paris in the early 1890s. The chain visible in the photograph on p. 82 is not the traction chain. It is prob-ably a slack mooring chain. The traction chain would be rather more substantial, and it would be picked up on the centreline of the tug, probably into a trough in the middle of the vessel where it would be taken round a friction drum — or per-haps a Fowler clip-drum. To pick up the traction chain at the point shown in the photograph is a mechanical absurdity and while it might conceivably work in a wide river it would be useless in a narrow waterway. RODNEY WEAVER

Vol 1 No 1 September 1980. 29 North London Railway 

(Revision of General Order No. 369) : Workmen's Tickets The above tickets are issued each weekday to and from any station between Chalk Farm, Poplar and Broad Street, inclusive, at a fare of 2d. each. Each ticket is available for the day of issue only, and for one journey only in each direction, by the advertised workmen's trains, in third class carriages, and subject as regards luggage to the same regulations as other third class passengers. The tickets are available at any of the stations named thereon, or at any inter-mediate station; they must be shown to the Company's servants when required, and one half given up at the end of each journey. The ticket is a common one, available to either Chalk Farm, Poplar or Broad Street, or any intermediate station indifferently. Thus, for instance, a workman desirous of a ticket between Homerton and Haggerston will have issued to him a ticket available, at option, to or from any station between Chalk Farm, Poplar and Broad Street inclusive, but for one journey only in each direction. These tickets are issued subject to the provisions of the Company's Act, 30 Vic., cap 78, and use by the holder is evidence of a special contract upon these conditions. The tickets have a distinct colour for each day so as to facilitate the work of the collectors in detecting expired tickets; and collectors and examiners should keep a sharp look-out for tickets out of date, and if presented the ordinary local single fare to be charged. For the information of the staff generally, patterns of the tickets, also the days of the week on which they are issued, are given below: 

Monday's issue (Inward) 

Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday 

Light Brown Green Dark Brown Grey Drab Vermilion Colours of all outward are orange. Chief booking clerks, and senior clerks, where there is no chief clerk, will be held 

personally responsible for tickets of the correct colour being issued each day, as in case of mistake disputes will arise between the ticket collectors and the holder of the tickets. The tickets, which are restricted to artisans, mechanics, and daily labourers, are to be issued to persons whose appearance at once denotes them to be bona fide 

workmen, without any inquiry being made, but when from their dress, &c., they may appear to be employed as clerks, &c., particulars of their employment should be obtained, and forwarded to the Traffic Superintendent on one of the forms supplied for the purpose. By the term 'daily labourers' it is intended to include warehouse porters and others who receive a weekly wage, but no one employed on an annual salary. The arrangements are also applicable to workwomen as well as men. Last Trains: Poplar to Broad Street, 7.31 from Poplar, 7.40 local to Bow. Chalk Farm to Broad Street, 7.29 Chalk Farm, 7.42 local from C anonbury . Broad Street to Poplar, 7.35 from Broad Street. Return by any Ordinary Chalk Farm, Bow Local or Poplar train after 12 noon. Passengers are allowed to pass barriers before 12 noon if weather wet etc. 31 March 1908. 30 Obituary: Geoffrey H. Platt 

We regret to record the death, on 25 July last, of Geoffrey Platt, in his 71st year, who had been a member of this Society since 1962. He had a wide range of interests, and would discuss any railway subject with enthusiasm, although his main loyalty was to the London & North Western Railway, and to the north west of England generally. He joined the Manchester Model Railway Club in 1928 and became one of the best-known of model railway enthusiasts, becoming President of that Society in 1975. He achieved high academic and professional status and in 1947 was appointed Lecturer in Electrical Engineering at King's College, London University, where in due course he was Sub-Dean of the Faculty of Electrical Engineering for almost twenty years. He was a modest man and his professional career was known to very few people and, as recorded in an appreciation in The Link, journal of the Manchester Model Railway Society, 'even fewer ever heard him mention it'. From time to time he contributed correspondence to the Journal of the R&CHS, a letter on the Melingriffith Waterwheel appearing in July 1980. He was always ready — as the writer remembers — to correspond and answer questions, and to give help whenever he could. The Editor is indebted to Mr. W.H.Tate of the Manchester Model Railway Society for much of the information in this note. 

# Important Notes 

This issue (Vol. XXVII No. 1) is the first issue of an enlarged volume which will extend over the years 1981, 1982, and 1983, and will consist of nine issues of the Journal. The volume will be fully indexed at the end of this period. As most members will know by now, Mr. Jeoffry Spence is handing over editorial duties to Mr. John V. Gough, subject to confirmation at the A.G.M. Please help Mr. Gough, whose address is 12 Victoria Gardens, 195 London Road, Leicester LE2 1ZH by sending him material (typed double-spacing with a left-hand margin of 11/2 inches) not later than 10 April for the July 1981 issue. Articles should be complete with any photographs, plans, maps, tables etc. Charges for advertisements: £15 full page and £10 half p7ge. Remittance should be sent, with camera-ready copy, to Mr. Pat McCarthy, 6 Carisbrooke Close, Wistaston, Crewe CW2 8JD. All material published in the Journal is copyright and must not be reproduced without the permission of the Editor. Views expressed in any article or item of correspondence in this or any other Journal of the R&CHS are not necessarily those of the Editor or of the Railway & Canal Historical Society. **Victoria station**, also known as **London Victoria**, is a [central London railway terminus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_station_group "London station group") and connected [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground") station in [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_London "Victoria, London"), in the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster"), managed by [Network Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_Rail "Network Rail").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-3) Named after the nearby [Victoria Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_names_of_Pimlico_and_Victoria "Street names of Pimlico and Victoria"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-4) the mainline station is a terminus of the [Brighton Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_Main_Line "Brighton Main Line") to [Gatwick Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport_railway_station "Gatwick Airport railway station") and [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_railway_station "Brighton railway station") and the [Chatham Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Main_Line "Chatham Main Line") to [Ramsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsgate_railway_station "Ramsgate railway station") and [Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_Priory_railway_station "Dover Priory railway station") via [Chatham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_railway_station,_Medway "Chatham railway station, Medway"). From the main lines, trains can connect to the [Catford Loop Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catford_Loop_Line "Catford Loop Line"), the [Dartford Loop Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartford_Loop_Line "Dartford Loop Line"), the [Sutton & Mole Valley lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_%26_Mole_Valley_lines "Sutton & Mole Valley lines") to [Dorking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorking_railway_station "Dorking railway station") and the [Oxted line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxted_line "Oxted line") to [East Grinstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Grinstead_railway_station "East Grinstead railway station"). [Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_(train_operating_company) "Southern (train operating company)") operates most commuter and regional services to south London, Sussex and parts of east Surrey and south-east Hampshire while [Southeastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_(train_operating_company) "Southeastern (train operating company)") operates trains to south-east London and Kent, alongside limited services operated by [Thameslink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thameslink "Thameslink"). [Gatwick Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Express "Gatwick Express") trains run direct to Gatwick. The London Underground station is served by three lines: [Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_line_(London_Underground) "Circle line (London Underground)"), [District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_line "District line") and [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_line "Victoria line"). On the Circle and District lines, the station is between [Sloane Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sloane_Square_tube_station "Sloane Square tube station") and [St James's Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James%27s_Park_tube_station "St James's Park tube station") stations. On the Victoria line, it is between [Pimlico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pimlico_tube_station "Pimlico tube station") and [Green Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Park_tube_station "Green Park tube station") stations. The area around the station is an important interchange for other forms of transport: a local bus station is in the forecourt and [Victoria Coach Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Coach_Station "Victoria Coach Station") is nearby, which serves national and international coaches.

Victoria was built to serve both the Brighton and Chatham Main Lines, and has always had a "split" feel of being two separate stations. The Brighton station opened in 1860 with the Chatham station following two years later. It replaced a temporary terminus at [Pimlico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosvenor_Road_railway_station#Pimlico "Grosvenor Road railway station"), and construction involved building the [Grosvenor Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosvenor_Bridge "Grosvenor Bridge") over the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames"). It became immediately popular as a [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") terminus, causing delays and requiring upgrades and rebuilding. It was well known for luxury [Pullman train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pullman_train_(UK) "Pullman train (UK)") services and continental boat-train trips, and became a focal point for soldiers during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").

As at other London termini, steam trains were phased out of Victoria by the 1960s, to be replaced by suburban electric and [diesel multiple-unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diesel_multiple-unit "Diesel multiple-unit") services; all services from the station are currently operated using [third rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_rail "Third rail") electric multiple units. Despite the end of international services following the opening of the [Channel Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_Tunnel "Channel Tunnel"), Victoria still remains an important London terminal station. The [connected Underground station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_tube_station "Victoria tube station"), in particular, suffered from overcrowding, until a major upgrade was completed in the late 2010s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-5) Gatwick Express provides half-hourly non-stop direct services between London Victoria and Gatwick Airport. However [Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_(Govia_Thameslink_Railway) "Southern (Govia Thameslink Railway)") run more frequent semi-fast services to [Gatwick Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport_railway_station "Gatwick Airport railway station").

The station complex is in [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_London "Victoria, London") in the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster "City of Westminster"), immediately south of the [London Inner Ring Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Inner_Ring_Road "London Inner Ring Road"). It is located south of Victoria Street, east of [Buckingham Palace Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace_Road "Buckingham Palace Road") and west of [Vauxhall Bridge Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vauxhall_Bridge_Road "Vauxhall Bridge Road").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-6) Several railways lead into the station line by way of [Grosvenor Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosvenor_Bridge "Grosvenor Bridge") from the south west, south and south east.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaviesGrant198348-7) It is in [London fare zone 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_fare_zone_1 "London fare zone 1") and is one of 19 stations managed by [Network Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_Rail "Network Rail").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-8) It has been a Grade II listed building since 1970.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-9)

[Victoria Coach Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Coach_Station "Victoria Coach Station") is about 300 metres south-west of the railway stations. It is the main London coach terminal and serves all parts of the UK and mainland Europe.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-10)

The station is served by a large number of [London Buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Buses "London Buses") routes day and night, using [Victoria bus station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_bus_station "Victoria bus station") or neighbouring streets.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-12)

By 1850, railways serving destinations to the south of London had three termini available – [London Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_railway_station "London Bridge railway station"), [Bricklayers' Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricklayers%27_Arms_railway_station "Bricklayers' Arms railway station") and [Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Waterloo_railway_station "London Waterloo railway station"). All three were inconvenient for [Central London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_London "Central London") as they terminated south of the river [Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames "Thames"), whereas the main centres of population, business and government were north of the river in the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London"), the [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London "West End of London") and [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984268-13)

Victoria Station was designed in a piecemeal fashion to help address this problem for the [London Brighton and South Coast Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Brighton_and_South_Coast_Railway "London Brighton and South Coast Railway") (LB&SCR) and the [London Chatham and Dover Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Chatham_and_Dover_Railway "London Chatham and Dover Railway") (LC&DR). It consisted of two adjacent main line railway stations which, from the viewpoint of passengers, were unconnected.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984267%E2%80%93268-14)

[![Image 18: A section of a vintage map showing Victoria Station and surrounding streets, with a mix of yellow, white, and black lines illustrating roads and railways](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/5c/Victoria_station_1897.jpg/250px-Victoria_station_1897.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victoria_station_1897.jpg)

Victoria Station in 1897, showing the separate Brighton (left) and Chatham (right) stations.

The [London and Brighton Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Brighton_Railway "London and Brighton Railway") terminus at [London Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_railway_station "London Bridge railway station") provided reasonable access to the City of London but was inconvenient for travellers to and from Westminster. As early as 1842 [John Urpeth Rastrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Urpeth_Rastrick "John Urpeth Rastrick") had proposed that the railway should build a branch to serve the West End, but his proposal was unsuccessful.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurner1978116%E2%80%93117-15)

However, the transfer of [the Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") from [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") to [Sydenham Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydenham_Hill "Sydenham Hill") between 1851 and 1854 created a major tourist attraction in the then rural area south of London, and the LB&SCR opened a [branch line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branch_line "Branch line") from the [Brighton Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_Main_Line "Brighton Main Line") at [Sydenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydenham,_London "Sydenham, London") to the site in 1854.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGray197742%E2%80%933-16) While this was under construction the [West End of London and Crystal Palace Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London_and_Crystal_Palace_Railway "West End of London and Crystal Palace Railway") also planned a line from Crystal Palace, to a new station at [Battersea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea "Battersea") Wharf, at the southern end of the new [Chelsea Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Bridge "Chelsea Bridge"). Despite its location, the new station was called Pimlico. It opened on 27 March 1858, but was very much regarded as a temporary terminus, composed of a small number of wooden huts, and positioned immediately next to a proposed bridge over the Thames.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984268-13) Shortly afterwards the LB&SCR leased most of the lines of the new railway, and built a further connection from Crystal Palace to the Brighton Main Line at [Norwood Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwood_Junction_railway_station "Norwood Junction railway station"), thereby providing itself with a route into west London, although it was recognised that a terminus would be needed on the north side of the river.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGray197742%E2%80%933-16)

[![Image 19: Diagram of the Clapham Junction and Stewarts Lane railway junction, as well as the neighboring Lavender Hill and Latchmere junctions, showcasing the complex track layout and signaling system](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Clapham_Junction%2C_Stewarts_Lane%2C_Lavender_Hill_%26_Longhedge_RJD_17.jpg/250px-Clapham_Junction%2C_Stewarts_Lane%2C_Lavender_Hill_%26_Longhedge_RJD_17.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clapham_Junction,_Stewarts_Lane,_Lavender_Hill_%26_Longhedge_RJD_17.jpg)

The approaches to Victoria Station in 1912. The line leading to the station is top right, the 'Brighton line' (shown in green) is bottom left and the 'Chatham line' (pink) bottom right. The connection to the GWR and LNWR (purple) is top left.

During the summer of 1857 a scheme for an independent "Grosvenor Basin Terminus" in the West End of London, "for the use of the Southern Railways of England" was mooted.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGray197744-17) The station was originally referred to as the "Grosvenor Terminus" but later renamed Victoria as it was sited at the end of Victoria Street.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGray197745-18) Three other railway companies were also seeking a terminus in Westminster: the [Great Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Western_Railway "Great Western Railway") (GWR), the [London & North Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_North_Western_Railway "London and North Western Railway") (LNWR), and the [East Kent Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Kent_Railway "East Kent Railway") (EKR). The first two already had rail access to Battersea through their joint ownership of the [West London Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_London_Line "West London Line") with the LB&SCR. In 1858, the EKR leased the remaining lines of the [West End of London and Crystal Palace Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London_and_Crystal_Palace_Railway "West End of London and Crystal Palace Railway") from [Shortlands railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortlands_railway_station "Shortlands railway station"), and also negotiated temporary running powers over the lines recently acquired by the LB&SCR, pending the construction of its own line into west London.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurner1978121-19) On 23 July 1859 these four companies together formed the [Victoria Station and Pimlico Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Station_and_Pimlico_Railway "Victoria Station and Pimlico Railway") (VS&PR) company, with the object of extending the railway from [Stewarts Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stewarts_Lane "Stewarts Lane") Junction, Battersea across the river to a more convenient location nearer the West End,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurner1978122-20) and the following month the EKR changed its name to the [London Chatham and Dover Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Chatham_and_Dover_Railway "London Chatham and Dover Railway").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984269-21)

The new line followed part of the route of the [Grosvenor Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosvenor_Canal "Grosvenor Canal") with Victoria station on the former canal basin. It required the construction of a new bridge over the Thames, originally known as Victoria Bridge and later as Grosvenor Bridge.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984269-21) The bridge was 930 feet (280 m) long, which was required so that it could clear all river traffic. It was designed by [John Fowler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_John_Fowler,_1st_Baronet "Sir John Fowler, 1st Baronet"). The line was built as mixed [gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_gauge "Rail gauge") from Longhedge Junction, Battersea, to cater for GWR trains. It required a 1-in-50 climb and a 15 chains (990 ft; 300 m) turn from the LSWR main line to reach the bridge.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984271-22) The LB&SCR had hoped to amalgamate with the VS&PR, and introduced a parliamentary bill to allow it to do so in 1860. This was opposed by the GWR and LC&DR and rejected.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-23) By way of compromise the LB&SCR was permitted to lease Victoria station from the VS&PR, but agreed to accommodate the other railways until a terminus could be built for them on an adjoining site.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984271-22)

[![Image 20: A map of the Victoria Station in London, with various streets and buildings labeled](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/DISTRICT%281888%29_p142_-_Victoria_Station_%28plan%29.jpg/250px-DISTRICT%281888%29_p142_-_Victoria_Station_%28plan%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DISTRICT(1888)_p142_-_Victoria_Station_(plan).jpg)

Plan of Victoria Station as it was in 1888. The 'Chatham' side was rebuilt in 1906 and the 'Brighton' side in 1898–1908

The LB&SCR side of Victoria station opened on 1 October 1860, the temporary terminus in Battersea having closed the day before. The station was designed by [Robert Jacomb-Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jacomb-Hood "Robert Jacomb-Hood").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984272-24) It consisted of six platforms and ten tracks, with an entrance on Victoria Street. The site then covered 8.5 acres (3.4 ha)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGordon1910157-25) and was 800 feet (240 m) long and 230 feet (70 m) wide. The roof was built on a set of wrought iron girders, with an additional safety row that would allow the main girders to withstand a train strike.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984272-24) On the northwest corner of the station was the 300-bedroom [Grosvenor Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clermont,_Victoria "The Clermont, Victoria"). It was designed by J. T. Knowles, and run independently of the station itself. It opened in 1861.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984274-26) The LCDR and GWR opened their own station on 25 August 1862, occupying a less imposing wooden-fronted building with an entrance on Wilton Road.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBody1989201-27) The Chatham line station had eight platforms, five of which were of mixed gauge, shared by [broad-gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad-gauge "Broad-gauge") trains of the GWR from [Windsor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_%26_Eton_Central_railway_station "Windsor & Eton Central railway station") via [Southall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southall_railway_station "Southall railway station").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-ReferenceA-28)

Victoria station proved to be unexpectedly popular for both the main companies, and by 1862 there were frequent delays due to congestion at Stewarts Lane Junction. In March 1863 the LB&SCR and the LC&DR jointly funded a new high-level route into Victoria, avoiding Stewarts Lane and requiring the widening of Grosvenor Bridge, including the replacement of the broad-gauge rails with a third LB&SCR line. The work was completed during 1867/8.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGray197761-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984278-30) The [South Eastern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Eastern_Railway_(UK) "South Eastern Railway (UK)") (SER) wanted to use Victoria as a London terminus as it was more convenient than London Bridge, but were advised they would need to pay extensive tolls and expenses to do so. Consequently, the SER constructed a station at [Charing Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charing_Cross_railway_station "Charing Cross railway station") instead.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGray1990111-31)

The GWR began services on 1 April 1863, connecting Victoria to Southall, and later some services to [Uxbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uxbridge_Vine_Street_railway_station "Uxbridge Vine Street railway station"), [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading_railway_station "Reading railway station"), [Slough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slough_railway_station "Slough railway station") and Windsor.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984274-26) From 13 August 1866 the LB&SCR ran services from Victoria to London Bridge along the newly completed [South London Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_London_Line "South London Line").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984278-30) The [Great Northern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_Railway_(Great_Britain) "Great Northern Railway (Great Britain)") began a service from Victoria to [Barnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Barnet_railway_station "New Barnet railway station") (via [Ludgate Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludgate_Hill_railway_station "Ludgate Hill railway station")) on 1 March 1868, with other cross-London services running via Victoria in the 1870s.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984277-32)

In 1898 the LB&SCR decided to demolish its station and replace it with an enlarged red-brick Renaissance-style building, designed by [Charles Langbridge Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Langbridge_Morgan_(engineer) "Charles Langbridge Morgan (engineer)").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBetjeman197298-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGordon1910157%E2%80%938-34) Since widening of the station was prevented by the LC&DR station and Buckingham Palace Road, increased capacity was achieved by lengthening the platforms and building [crossovers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_(rail) "Crossover (rail)") to allow two trains to use each platform simultaneously.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-Bonavia_(1987)-35) Work was completed in 1908, and included the rebuilding of the Grosvenor Hotel at the same time. The site then covered 16 acres (6.5 ha) with 2.25 miles (3.62 km) of platforms.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGordon1910157-25) Overhead electric trains began to run into Victoria on 1 December 1909, to London Bridge. The line to [Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Palace_railway_station "Crystal Palace railway station") was electrified on 12 May 1911.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurner1979172%E2%80%935-36)

Victoria became well known for its [Pullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pullman_train_(UK) "Pullman train (UK)") services during the late 19th century. The LB&SCR introduced the first Pullman first-class service to Brighton on 1 November 1875, followed by the first all-Pullman train in the UK on 1 December 1881.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984267-37) Another all-Pullman service was introduced in 1908 under the name of the Southern Belle, then described as "... the most luxurious train in the world...".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin201488-38) The SECR began Pullman continental services on 21 April 1910 and on domestic services to the Kent coast on 16 June 1919. The [Golden Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Arrow_(train) "Golden Arrow (train)"), another all-Pullman train began services in 1924, and remained in service until 30 September 1972.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984267%E2%80%93268-14)

[![Image 21: Facade of Victoria Station in London, with people walking around](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Victoria_Station_London%2C_Southern_Railway_Building_%28geograph_1201572%29.jpg/250px-Victoria_Station_London%2C_Southern_Railway_Building_%28geograph_1201572%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victoria_Station_London,_Southern_Railway_Building_(geograph_1201572).jpg)

The London Chatham and Dover Station as rebuilt by the South Eastern and Chatham Railway.

The LC&DR and GWR jointly leased the 'Chatham' portion of the station for 999 years from 28 June 1860, with the GWR responsible for 6.67%.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-ReferenceA-28) The LC&DR completed its main line as far as [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury") on 3 December 1860 and began to use the LB&SCR station on that day.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-White_1961-39)

[![Image 22: Steam train is shown at a station with a large domed roof](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Victoria_%28Eastern_Section%29_Station%2C_with_SR_2-6-0_working_empty_stock_geograph-2638200-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg/250px-Victoria_%28Eastern_Section%29_Station%2C_with_SR_2-6-0_working_empty_stock_geograph-2638200-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victoria_(Eastern_Section)_Station,_with_SR_2-6-0_working_empty_stock_geograph-2638200-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg)

The Eastern side in 1958

From 1899 the LC&DR entered a working union with its rival, the [South Eastern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Eastern_Railway_(UK) "South Eastern Railway (UK)"), to form the [South Eastern and Chatham Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Eastern_and_Chatham_Railway "South Eastern and Chatham Railway") (SECR). As a result, services from its station at Victoria began to be rationalised and integrated with those from the other SECR termini.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGray199052-40)

The LC&DR station began to be reconstructed in the late 19th century after several properties on Buckingham Palace Road, and the hotel, were bought by the company. Work began in 1899 with the removal of the old roof.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984281-41) The rebuilt station was partially opened on 10 June 1906, with additional platforms and cab exit on 10 February the following year, along with a new annexe to the hotel. It was formally re-opened on 1 July 1908.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984282-42) As a consequence of the rebuilding, [boat trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boat_train "Boat train") become more popular from Victoria compared to Charing Cross and Cannon Street. Services increased to serve Ostend and Calais via Dover and Rotterdam via Gravesend. The LB&SCR part of the station also served Dieppe via Newhaven.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984287-43)

Victoria has since seen more visits from royalty and heads of state than any other London station. During the [funeral of Edward VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Edward_VII "Death and state funeral of Edward VII"), seven kings, over 20 princes and five archdukes were greeted here.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeinrebHibbertKeayKeay2008975-44)

In the early 20th century, the development and improvement of the [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground"), meant that Victoria could not compete as a cross-London service. GNR trains stopped running on 1 October 1907, with Midland ones following in June the next year. The GWR ceased to use the station for scheduled services on 21 March 1915, partly due to [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") in addition to the new Underground lines. Victoria was used as the main station for drafted soldiers, and those returning from action in the war. By the middle of the war, the station served twelve trains a day running between Victoria and Folkestone, with additional trains serving Dover. The station was regularly served with a voluntary buffet for departing soldiers, who served up to 4,000 men a day.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984288-45) Victoria itself did not suffer significant damage during the war, but a section of Grosvenor Bridge was destroyed after an anti-aircraft shell struck a gas main underneath it.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984239-46)

Following the war, memorials were built on both parts of the station. The Southern Railway side marks 626 soldiers killed or missing, while the Chatham side marks 556.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984289-47) A plaque marks the arrival of the body of [The Unknown Warrior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Unknown_Warrior "The Unknown Warrior") at Victoria on 10 November 1920.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-48)

The service to [Ostend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostend "Ostend") via Dover was re-introduced on 18 January 1919. Civilian trains to [Boulogne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulogne "Boulogne") via Folkestone restarted on 3 February. Boat train services to [Newhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newhaven_Marine_railway_station "Newhaven Marine railway station") started on 1 June, and a connection with Paris started on 15 July. On 8 January 1920, Victoria replaced Charing Cross as the main station for continental services, as it had more facilities and closer locomotive and carriage facilities. The service to Paris via Calais and Dover began on the same day.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984289-47)

[![Image 23: Crowded train station with signage, columns, and an arched entrance](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Victoria_%28Central%29_concourse_geograph-3004411-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg/250px-Victoria_%28Central%29_concourse_geograph-3004411-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victoria_(Central)_concourse_geograph-3004411-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg)

The Brighton side concourse in 1955

The two stations at Victoria came largely under single ownership in 1923 with the formation of the [Southern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Railway_(Great_Britain) "Southern Railway (Great Britain)") (SR) as part of the [Big Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Four_(British_railway_companies) "Big Four (British railway companies)") grouping.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984290-49) The following year steps were taken to integrate the two stations. The platforms were renumbered in a single sequence, openings were made in the wall separating them to allow passengers to pass from one to the other without going into the street, and alterations were made to the tracks to allow for interchangeable working.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDendy_Marshall1988396-50) The work was completed in 1925, and all platforms were renumbered in a contiguous sequence.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984290-49) Electric suburban services to Herne Hill and Orpington first ran on 12 July that year, followed by South London line services on 17 June 1928, and electric services to Crystal Palace and [Epsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epsom_railway_station "Epsom railway station") (via [Mitcham Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitcham_Junction_railway_station "Mitcham Junction railway station")) on 3 March 1929.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984291-51) The SR also concentrated continental steamer traffic at Victoria, introducing the Golden Arrow, in 1924,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984267-37) and the [Night Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_Ferry "Night Ferry") in 1936.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin2017182-52)

[![Image 24: Vintage black and white shot of a steam train at a train station, with passengers visible on the platform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Victoria_%28Central%29_Station_with_train_from_Tunbridge_Wells_West_geograph-2686103-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg/250px-Victoria_%28Central%29_Station_with_train_from_Tunbridge_Wells_West_geograph-2686103-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victoria_(Central)_Station_with_train_from_Tunbridge_Wells_West_geograph-2686103-by-Ben-Brooksbank.jpg)

The Central side in 1961 with train from Tunbridge Wells West

The station had a [news cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_cinema "News cinema") (later a cartoon cinema) that showed a continuous programme. The cinema was designed by Alister MacDonald, son of the Prime Minister [Ramsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsay_MacDonald "Ramsay MacDonald"), and was in operation from 1933 until it was demolished in 1981. The GWR remained part-owner of the station until 1932 thereafter retaining running powers, although it does not appear to have used them.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984368-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-54)

Night-train services stopped running from Victoria on 4 September 1939 after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") was declared, and other services were terminated following the German invasion of France in May 1940. Though the station was bombed several times in 1940 and 1941, there was not enough damage to prevent operations. A plane crashed into the eastern side of the station on 15 September 1940 and a flying bomb caused partial damage on 27 June 1944.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984294-55)

The greatest change to the station during the 1920s and 1930s was the introduction of [third-rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-rail "Third-rail")[electrification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_electrification_in_Great_Britain#650_V_-_850_V_DC,_Third_Rail_%22Southern_Electric%22 "Railway electrification in Great Britain") for all [suburban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") and many [main-line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_line_(railway) "Main line (railway)") services, replacing the original LB&SCR overhead scheme by 1929 and largely replacing steam traction, except on Chatham Section main-line and Oxted line trains. Services to [Orpington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpington_railway_station "Orpington railway station") were electrified in 1925 and to Epsom the following year. By 1932 the Brighton Main Line was electrified, quickly followed by those to other Sussex coastal towns and [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth "Portsmouth") by 1938.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoody196823%E2%80%9367-56) The brand name "Southern Electric" was applied to all these services. The [Brighton Belle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_Belle "Brighton Belle"), the first electric all-Pullman service in the world, ran from Victoria from 29 June 1934 until its withdrawal in 1972.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984368-53)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin201489-57)

[![Image 25: Black and white picture of a Golden Arrow train under a bridge](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/London_victoria_2052605_b6a388dc.jpg/250px-London_victoria_2052605_b6a388dc.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:London_victoria_2052605_b6a388dc.jpg)

The _[Golden Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden\_Arrow\_(train) "Golden Arrow (train)")_ leaving Victoria Station, 1953

[British Railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail "British Rail") (BR) took over the station on 1 January 1948. A new set of offices for Continental trains opened on 14 June, while the eastern booking hall was renovated, opening on 5 February 1951.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984294-55)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-58)

During the 1950s and early 1960s [British Railways (Southern Region)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Region_of_British_Railways "Southern Region of British Railways") completed its Kent Coast Electrification schemes, which meant that most of the remaining services from the station were electrified, including boat trains. Some minor services were withdrawn, and the few remaining steam services, to [Oxted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxted_railway_station "Oxted railway station") and beyond, were replaced by [diesel-electric multiple units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diesel_electric_multiple_unit "Diesel electric multiple unit").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984296-59) Various plans were proposed at this time to redevelop Victoria, including new offices, hotels and a helicopter station.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984295-60) The last steam service left Victoria on 8 January 1964 to [East Grinstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Grinstead_railway_station "East Grinstead railway station"), after which it was replaced by diesel-electric multiple units.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984296-59)

The station was redeveloped internally in the 1980s, with the addition of shops within the concourse, and above the western platforms as the "Victoria Place" shopping centre and 220,000 square feet (20,000 m 2) of office space. Platforms 16 and 17 opened on the site of the former taxi rank on 21 December 1987.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-62) A major re-signalling scheme was carried out during the works.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984368-53) The station was managed by [Network SouthEast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_SouthEast "Network SouthEast") also under British Rail.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJeffs20138-63)

[![Image 26: Red and yellow train stopped at a train station](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/460007_at_London_Victoria.jpg/250px-460007_at_London_Victoria.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:460007_at_London_Victoria.jpg)

[Gatwick Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Express "Gatwick Express") service at Victoria in 2003

The other major change to the station under BR was the gradual development of services to [Gatwick Airport station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport_railway_station "Gatwick Airport railway station") after its opening on 28 May 1958. A dedicated rail-air terminal opened on top of platform 15 on 1 May 1962, designed by Clive Pascall.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984296-59)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-64)

Several long-standing services from Victoria ended during the BR era. The _[Brighton Belle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton\_Belle "Brighton Belle")'_ s final service was on 30 April 1972, followed by the last _[Golden Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden\_Arrow\_(train) "Golden Arrow (train)")_ on 30 September. The _[Night Ferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night\_Ferry "Night Ferry")_ lasted until 31 October 1980, though the [Venice-Simplon Orient Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice-Simplon_Orient_Express "Venice-Simplon Orient Express"), a luxury Pullman service, has been running intermittently since 1982.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984368-53)

In 1984 the non-stop [Gatwick Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Express "Gatwick Express") service was started, aiming for a 30-minute journey time. This was coupled with the provision of an airport lounge and check-in facilities at first-floor level, with dedicated escalators down to the Gatwick Express platforms. [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") and other major airlines had their own check-in desks there.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984368%E2%80%93369-65) British Rail operated an International Travel Centre within the main station, separate from the domestic travel centre. At the time, Victoria was still a major departure point for international travel, with boat trains to [Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_Western_Docks_railway_station "Dover Western Docks railway station") and [Folkestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folkestone_Harbour_railway_station "Folkestone Harbour railway station") for France and Belgium and beyond.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984297-66) This ceased with the introduction of [Eurostar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurostar "Eurostar") in 1994, which did not serve Victoria, and the International Travel Centre closed.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChristopher2011101-67)

Victoria is a proposed stop on [Crossrail 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossrail_2 "Crossrail 2"), the route of which has been safeguarded since 1991.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-68) The project would involve the construction of two new 250-metre (820 ft) long platforms, and new entrances onto Ebury Street and the main National Rail station. The [District and Circle line ticket hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_tube_station "Victoria tube station") would be expanded and include a direct connection to the new Crossrail station. Crossrail 2 trains would also be able to reverse at Victoria. The service proposes to run 30 additional trains per hour through the station, which is expected to reduce crowding in Victoria by 25%.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-69)

In January 2020, Victoria BID – the local [Business improvement district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_improvement_district "Business improvement district") – proposed removing the bus station from the mainline station forecourt to create a new "Station Square". Bus stops would be relocated to nearby streets.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-71)

In 2024, Network Rail announced that architects [Hawkins\Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hawkins/Brown&action=edit&redlink=1 "Hawkins/Brown (page does not exist)") and [Acme Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acme_Space "Acme Space") had begun work on a future "major office-led redevelopment" of the station.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-72)

In 2019/20, Victoria was the [second-busiest station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_railway_stations_in_Great_Britain "List of busiest railway stations in Great Britain") in the UK, with an estimated 73.6 million passenger entries/exits.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-73) However, as with other stations, patronage dropped dramatically as a result of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). The estimated usage figure fell 81% in 2020/21 to 13.8 million, although Victoria retained its rank in second place, behind [Stratford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratford_railway_station "Stratford railway station").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-74)

Operationally, there are two separate main line [termini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminus_station "Terminus station"):

*   The eastern (Chatham) side, comprising platforms 1–8, is the terminus for [Southeastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_(train_operating_company) "Southeastern (train operating company)") services to [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent") on the [Chatham Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Main_Line "Chatham Main Line") and its branches.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-75) This is also the London terminus for the [Venice-Simplon Orient Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice-Simplon_Orient_Express "Venice-Simplon Orient Express"), from Platform 2, the longest platform.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-76) It was used for boat trains to Dover and Folkestone until these were made redundant by the introduction of [Eurostar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurostar "Eurostar") trains to the continent in 1994.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984287,_289-77)
*   The western (Brighton) side, comprising platforms 9–19, is the terminus for [Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_(train_operating_company) "Southern (train operating company)")[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-78) and Gatwick Express services to [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey"), [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex "Sussex") and parts of southern [Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire "Hampshire") including Gatwick Airport and Brighton on the Brighton Main Line and the East Grinstead branch on the [Oxted Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxted_Line "Oxted Line").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-southern-79)

Services are operated by Southeastern and Southern, owned by the [Department for Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Transport "Department for Transport") and [Govia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Govia "Govia")[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-80) respectively. All services at Victoria use electric multiple unit trains.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJackson1984291-51)

To help passengers choose the correct service, the floor of the main concourse at Victoria was marked with different coloured lines. Passengers could then follow the line marked with the specific colour for that service to arrive at their intended departure point.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-81)

[Southeastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_(train_operating_company) "Southeastern (train operating company)") services at Victoria use platforms 1–8. The station is served by a mixture of metro and long distance (mainline) services. Metro services are operated using [Class 465](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_465 "British Rail Class 465") and [466](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_466 "British Rail Class 466")[EMUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_multiple_unit "Electric multiple unit") whilst mainline services are operated using [Class 375](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_375 "British Rail Class 375") and [377](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_377 "British Rail Class 377") EMUs.

As of December 2024, the typical off-peak service operated by Southeastern in trains per hour (tph) is:[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-82)

*   4 tph to [Orpington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpington_railway_station "Orpington railway station") via [Beckenham Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckenham_Junction_station "Beckenham Junction station")
*   2 tph to [Gravesend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravesend_railway_station "Gravesend railway station") via [Bexleyheath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bexleyheath_railway_station "Bexleyheath railway station")
*   1 tph to [Ramsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsgate_railway_station "Ramsgate railway station") via [Faversham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faversham_railway_station "Faversham railway station")
*   1 tph to [Dover Priory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_Priory_railway_station "Dover Priory railway station") via Faversham
*   1 tph to [Gillingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillingham_railway_station_(Kent) "Gillingham railway station (Kent)") via [Chatham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_railway_station_(Kent) "Chatham railway station (Kent)")
*   1 tph to [Ashford International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashford_International_railway_station "Ashford International railway station") via [Maidstone East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maidstone_East_railway_station "Maidstone East railway station")

[Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_(Govia_Thameslink_Railway) "Southern (Govia Thameslink Railway)") services at Victoria use platforms 9-12 and 15-19 as of August 2022. The station is served by a mixture of metro and long-distance (mainline) services. Southern metro and mainline services are both operated by [Class 377](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_377 "British Rail Class 377")[EMUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_multiple_unit "Electric multiple unit") and Gatwick Express is serviced by [Class 387](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_387 "British Rail Class 387") EMUs.

As of May 2025, the typical off-peak service operated by Southern in trains per hour (tph) is:[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-83)

*   2 tph to [London Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_station "London Bridge station") via [Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Palace_railway_station "Crystal Palace railway station")
*   2 tph to [Epsom Downs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epsom_Downs_railway_station "Epsom Downs railway station") via Sutton and [Norbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norbury_railway_station "Norbury railway station")
*   2 tph to [West Croydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Croydon_station "West Croydon station") via Crystal Palace
*   2 tph to [Dorking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorking_railway_station "Dorking railway station") via [Epsom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epsom_railway_station "Epsom railway station") and [Sutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_railway_station_(London) "Sutton railway station (London)") of which 1 continues to [Horsham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsham_railway_station "Horsham railway station")
*   2 tph to [East Grinstead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Grinstead_railway_station "East Grinstead railway station") via [Oxted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxted_railway_station "Oxted railway station")
*   2 tph to [Reigate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reigate_railway_station "Reigate railway station") via [Redhill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redhill_railway_station "Redhill railway station")
*   2 tph to [Bognor Regis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bognor_Regis_railway_station "Bognor Regis railway station") and [Portsmouth Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_Harbour_railway_station "Portsmouth Harbour railway station"), dividing at Horsham
*   2 tph to [Littlehampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlehampton_railway_station "Littlehampton railway station") via [Worthing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worthing_railway_station "Worthing railway station")
*   2 tph to [Eastbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastbourne_railway_station "Eastbourne railway station") via [Lewes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewes_railway_station "Lewes railway station") of which 1 continues to [Ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ore_railway_station "Ore railway station")

During the suspension of the [Gatwick Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Express "Gatwick Express"), Southern services at Victoria began to use Platforms 13 and 14 as well as operating the Gatwick Express fleet of [Class 387](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_387 "British Rail Class 387") units. Gatwick Express services were reinstated in March 2022.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-GTW2020-84)

[Gatwick Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Express "Gatwick Express"), formerly a separate franchise but now operated by Southern, runs services from platforms 13 and 14. Ticket barriers were installed on these platforms in 2011.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-85)

As of September 2022, the typical off-peak service run by Gatwick Express in trains per hour (tph) is:

*   2 tph to [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_railway_station "Brighton railway station") (calling only at [Gatwick Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport_railway_station "Gatwick Airport railway station") and [Haywards Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haywards_Heath_railway_station "Haywards Heath railway station"))[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-86)

In the peak hours, Gatwick Express services call at intermediate stations between Haywards Heath and Brighton such as [Preston Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Park_railway_station "Preston Park railway station"), [Hassocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassocks_railway_station "Hassocks railway station") and [Burgess Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgess_Hill_railway_station "Burgess Hill railway station").

London Underground station
--------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=London_Victoria_station&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: London Underground station")]

[![Image 30: Entrance to Victoria Underground Station in London, with modern architecture in the background](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/201909_london_victoria_underground_station.jpg/250px-201909_london_victoria_underground_station.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:201909_london_victoria_underground_station.jpg)

Entrance to the tube station at Cardinal Place

There are two connected Underground stations at Victoria, on different levels and built more than a century apart. The older one, on the north side of the bus station, serves the [Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_line_(London_Underground) "Circle line (London Underground)") and [District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_line "District line") lines, constructed by ['cut and cover'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunnel#Cut-and-cover "Tunnel") methods just below road level. The newer station, closer to the main line station, serves the [Victoria line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_line "Victoria line"), a [deep-level tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_level_underground "Deep level underground"). Each has its own ticket hall, and the two are connected by a pedestrian passage beneath the bus station.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-87)

Victoria is currently the 3rd busiest station on the London Underground with 62.69 million passengers using the station in 2024.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-auto-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-:1-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victoria_station#cite_note-:2-90)
